F-actin was stained with phalloidin (red), nuclei were stained with DAPI (blue), and cell boundaries were visualized by DIC. Scale bar, 3 mum. D, E Wound healing assay of RAW 264.7 macrophages. Cells were infected for 2 h at an MOI of 50 with the indicated L. pneumophila strains. After a wound was created, representative images were taken at 2 h and 24 h post-wounding (D), and the wound healing rate was quantified (E). Data are mean +- SD (n = 3) and analyzed by one-way ANOVA. F Expression of SidG in the L. pneumophila strains was analyzed by immunoblotting with anti-Flag antibodies. ICDH served as a loading control. Data shown in F are representative from three independent experiments.

As the Arp2/3 complex orchestrates fundamental cellular processes, particularly cell migration, we examined the impact of SidG on cell motility by ectopic expression of SidG in host cells. Wild-type SidG, but not functionally inactive SidGH57A mutant, potently suppressed cellular motility without compromising cell viability (S10 Fig). We further determined whether the observed phenotype by SidG occurs under physiological conditions and found that wild-type bacteria efficiently inhibited cell migration while a mutant missing SidG (DeltasidG) lost the ability to affect host cell motility during L. pneumophila infection (Fig 6D-Fig 6D and 6F). Overexpression of SidG in a DeltasidG strain resulted in a more potent inhibition of cell migration compared to the wild-type strain (Fig 6D-F). Thus, SidG targets the Arp2/3 complex to disrupt cytoskeletal architecture and subvert motility programs.

passages.text: A structural model of SidG-Arp2/3 revealed that the C-terminal of ArpC2 positions near the Cys-His-Asp pocket of SidG (Fig 7A), which raised the possibility that SidG may modify ArpC2. Unfortunately, we neither observed any shift bands of ArpC2 by co-expression of SidG (S11A Fig) nor detected any modification of ArpC2 mediated by SidG via mass spectrometric analysis. This discrepancy might suggest that the predicted proximity is coincidental, or it could reflect the inherent limitations in the accuracy of in silico structural predictions for large, multi-protein complexes. To further elucidate the mechanisms of cytoskeletal disruption by SidG via the Arp2/3 complex, we conducted a suppressor screening by individually co-expressing each of the seven Arp2/3 complex subunits in yeast expressing SidG. Strikingly, only ArpC3 overexpression completely rescued SidG-mediated yeast growth inhibition (Fig 7B). Despite extensive efforts, we were unable to detect SidG-induced modification of ArpC3 (S11B and S11C Fig). These findings suggest that SidG may modulate Arp2/3 through a non-covalent mechanism, potentially exploiting ArpC3 subunit as the critical regulatory node akin to the mechanisms mediated by WASF-family NPFs and Arpin.
The Arp2/3 subunit ArpC3 suppresses the yeast toxicity of SidG.

passages.text: L. pneumophila employs SidG to enhance invasion

Next, we investigated the roles of SidG in the life cycle of L. pneumophila during infection. Previous studies identified SidG as a Dot/Icm substrate capable of interbacterial protein transfer, implying that this effector is expressed and competent for translocation during the infectious stationary phase. To validate this pioneer effector characteristic and examine its spatiotemporal regulation, we tracked SidG dynamics during the initial phase of infection using a SidG-overexpression strain. Consistent with a pre-formed effector primed for immediate action, SidG was rapidly recruited to the LCV. The proportion of SidG-positive vacuoles increased sharply following infection initiation, peaking at around 30 mins post-bacterial uptake (Fig 8A and 8B). Furthermore, LCVs containing wild-type, DeltasidG(pSidG) and DeltasidG(pSidGH57A) L. pneumophila efficiently recruited Rac1 to their surface in the early infection phase, while vacuoles harboring DeltasidG mutant showed significantly reduced recruitment of Rac1 (Fig 8C and 8E), which is consistent with our results that SidG binds to Rac1 independent of the SidG Cys-His-Asp motif. Despite only modest recruitment of ArpC3 to the LCVs (Fig 8D), SidG overexpression significantly enhanced Arp2/3-dependent membrane ruffling at L. pneumophila invasion sites (Fig 8F and 8G), along with the increased actin encasement of intracellular bacteria (Fig 8H and 8I). These findings collectively suggest that L. pneumophila actively promotes host cell invasion through SidG-mediated cytoskeletal rearrangements. To further assess the physiological significance of SidG in bacterial infection, we quantified intracellular L. pneumophila at 10 minutes post-infection. Importantly, the DeltasidG mutant strain exhibited significantly impaired cellular invasion compared to wild-type bacteria. Complementation with wild-type SidG, but not SidGH57A or the Rac1-binding defective SidGL867A/L877A mutant, restored the invasive capacity of the DeltasidG strain (Fig 8J). Consistently, further analysis revealed that SidG specifically accelerates the kinetics of bacterial internalization during the early stages of infection (S12 Fig).
SidG facilitates host cell invasion in the initial phase of bacterial infection.

We also examined the effect of SidG in intracellular replication of L. pneumophila by performing infection in bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and the protozoan host Dictyostelium discoideum. Consistent with previous studies, the DeltasidG mutant grew at rates indistinguishable from those of the wild-type strain in both laboratory infection models (S13A and S13B Fig). Also, sidG deletion did not affect the proportion of replicative LCVs (S13C and S13D Fig), suggesting that SidG is not required for the formation of the replication vacuoles. Taken together, these results indicate that SidG promotes L. pneumophila invasion but is dispensable for its intracellular replication.
Discussion

To successfully colonize host cells, intracellular bacterial pathogens must establish and maintain a stable replicative niche. This process critically depends on their ability to manipulate the host cytoskeleton, particularly by hijacking actin dynamics to control membrane remodeling, vesicular trafficking, and niche stability. Through evolutionary adaptation, bacteria have developed two principal mechanistic strategies to hijack host actin dynamics. The first strategy is to directly modulate actin functions by post-translational modifications. For example, the Clostridium botulinum C2 toxin and Photorhabdus luminescens Tc toxin affect actin polymerization by ADP-ribosylation. The Vibrio and Aeromonas ACD toxin cross-links actin monomers and thus prevents actin polymerization. Some pathogens impair the host cytoskeleton by direct proteolytic cleavage of actin, including grimelysin and protealysin from Serratia species and the Legionella effector RavK . Another strategy involves targeting or mimicking host regulatory proteins that control actin dynamics. Listeria monocytogenes ActA and Burkholderia BimA exploit their WH2 domains to functionally imitate host nucleators, facilitating actin nucleation, elongation, and filament bundling. Similarly, Vibrio VopF/VopL utilize tandem WH2 domains for dual activities in pointed-end actin elongation and nucleation, while Rickettsia Sca2 uniquely mimics formins by specifically promoting barbed-end elongation. Alternatively, pathogens target host actin nucleators or regulatory proteins. Shigella IcsB and Vibrio MARTX toxins subvert Rho GTPases through Nepsilon-fatty acylation, while L. pneumophila LegK2 phosphorylates the Arp3/ArpC1B subunits of the Arp2/3 complex. In this study, our findings reveal SidG as a novel T4SS effector that uniquely integrates both Rac1-dependent signaling and Arp2/3 complex modulation to mediate host cytoskeleton remodeling during L. pneumophila infection.

While a recent study had identified the Cys-His-Asp triad in SidG, our integrated bioinformatic and functional analyses also defined key structural residues, such as W32 and W148, that are requisite for the triad-mediated function. Importantly, we further elucidated a molecular switch governing the function of SidG. We propose a multi-step model in which SidG is maintained in a quiescent state until its C-terminal domain engages the host GTPase Rac1. The association of Rac1 not only releases auto-inhibition by liberating the N-terminal domain but also likely induces an allosteric conformational change that stabilizes the functional configuration of the Cys-His-Asp triad. This explains why the truncated SidG1-797, despite being capable of binding the Arp2/3 complex, fails to exhibit toxicity to yeast. This host factor-dependent activation strategy mirrors the regulatory logic employed by other Legionella effectors, such as SidJ and VipD, which rely on host Calmodulin and Rab GTPases, respectively. Such a mechanism effectively licenses bacterial effector activity exclusively within the eukaryotic cytosol, imposing a strict spatiotemporal checkpoint to prevent premature activation. The activated conformation then engages the Arp2/3 complex with ArpC3 subunit as the key factor, as evidenced by genetic suppression of SidG-induced yeast toxicity upon ArpC3 overexpression. Crucially, while the Cys-His-Asp triad is biochemically essential, we observed no evidence of Arp2/3 component cleavage or modification. Therefore, we suggest that SidG modulates Arp2/3 complex activity through a mechanism that does not involve detectable covalent modification, potentially via allosteric modulation, with ArpC3 serving as the critical regulatory node in this pathogen-host interface. Furthermore, while SidG is lethal to yeast, it inhibits mammalian cell migration without compromising viability. We attribute this discrepancy to distinct physiological and temporal contexts: actin polymerization is indispensable for yeast division and proliferation, whereas SidG-mediated cytoskeletal disruption in mammalian cells specifically impairs motility while cellular metabolism remains intact during acute expression. This confirms that the observed migration defect is a direct consequence of cytoskeletal perturbation rather than a secondary effect of cell toxicity.

passages.text: Our study establishes SidG as a distinctive addition to the extensive arsenal of cytoskeletal effectors employed by L. pneumophila, which also includes VipA, MavH, WipA, Ceg14, RavK, and LegK2. Although dispensable for intracellular bacterial replication, SidG's distinct role in facilitating invasion, coupled with its rapid spatiotemporal recruitment to the LCV, defines it as a pioneer effector tailored for the nascent stages of infection. A key limitation of the current study remains the incomplete understanding of the precise mechanism mediated by the Cys-His-Asp triad. Future investigations dissecting the molecular basis of this motif will be essential to fully resolve this sophisticated strategy of SidG-mediated cytoskeletal subversion.
Materials and methods
Ethics statement
The animal study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Jilin University (permit number: SY202412058).
Plasmids and bacterial strains

The bacterial strains and plasmids used in this study are detailed in S1 and S2 Tables, respectively. Primers are listed in S3 Table. Escherichia coli strains were routinely cultured at 37 C in Luria-Bertani (LB) broth or on LB agar plates supplemented with appropriate antibiotics. All L. pneumophila strains used were derived from the parental strain Lp02, and harbor the pZL507 plasmid to complement the thyA auxotrophy. L. pneumophila was cultured on CYE agar plates or in AYE broth. Both media were supplemented with 400 mg/L L-cysteine and 100 mg/L ferric nitrate. Liquid cultures were grown at 37 C with shaking at 220 rpm to the post-exponential phase (OD600 = 3.3-3.8) before use. The sidG deletion mutant (Lp02DeltasidG) was constructed using the suicide vector pSR47S via allelic exchange, following previously described methods. Briefly, the upstream and downstream flanking regions of the sidG gene were amplified from Lp02 genomic DNA using specific primer pairs (S3 Table). These fragments were subsequently joined by overlap extension PCR to generate a deletion allele. The PCR product was digested with BamHI and SalI and ligated into the corresponding sites of pSR47S. For complementation experiments, the coding sequence of sidG was cloned into the vector pZL507. The resulting plasmid was introduced into the corresponding mutant strain by electroporation. For protein expression in mammalian cells, the relevant coding sequences were PCR-amplified and subcloned into expression vectors including pEGFP-C1, pCMV-HA, or pCMV-Flag.
Cell culture and transfection

HeLa, HEK293, and HEK293T cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Cells were maintained in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 37 C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. BMDMs were prepared from A/J mice as previously described. All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Jilin University (permit number: SY202412058). For transient expression of exogenous proteins, cells were seeded in 6-well plates and transfected at approximately 80% confluency. Per well, 2.5 mug of total plasmid DNA was delivered using 3.5 muL Lipofectamine 3000 reagent and 3.5 muL P3000 reagent (Invitrogen), following the manufacturer's instructions.
Recombinant protein expression and purification

Recombinant GST-tagged Rac1 and PAK1 PBD proteins were expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells. Transformed cells were initially grown overnight at 37 C in LB medium containing 100 microg/mL ampicillin. This culture was then diluted 1:200 into 1 L of fresh LB-ampicillin medium and cultivated at 37 C with shaking until reaching OD600 of 0.6-0.8. Protein expression was subsequently induced with 0.1 mM IPTG (isopropyl beta-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside) and incubated for 16-18 h at 18 C with shaking. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4,000 x g for 20 minutes at 4 C. The resulting pellet was resuspended in ice-cold PBS supplemented with protease inhibitors and 1 mM DTT, and then lysed using a homogenizer (JN-mini, JNBIO, Guangzhou, China). Cell debris was removed by centrifugation at 12,000 x g for 30 minutes at 4 C to obtain the soluble lysate. The soluble fraction was incubated with Glutathione Agarose Resin (Sangon Biotech, Shanghai, China) for 2 h at 4 C with gentle rotation to facilitate binding. Bound GST-tagged proteins were eluted with 10 mM reduced glutathione (GSH). Finally, eluted fractions were pooled and subjected to two rounds of dialysis against storage buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 10% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT) at 4 C.
Yeast manipulation and toxicity assays

passages.text: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain used in this study was W303. Yeast strains were typically grown at 30 C in rich YPD medium (1% yeast extract, 2% peptone, 2% dextrose). For plasmid selection, transformants were grown on synthetic defined (SD) medium lacking the appropriate nutrient corresponding to the plasmid auxotrophic marker, specifically uracil for pSB157M or leucine for p425GPD. Yeast transformation was performed using the standard lithium acetate/single-stranded carrier DNA/PEG method.

The homozygous RHO5 deletion strain was generated using a PCR-based homologous recombination strategy. A deletion cassette containing the TRP1 marker flanked by 850 bp upstream and downstream homologous regions of RHO5 was generated and transformed into W303 cells. Transformants were selected on SD medium lacking tryptophan (SD/-Trp), and the deletion was verified by sequencing and RT-qPCR. Primers used for strain construction and RT-qPCR are listed in S3 Table.

To assess toxicity, overnight cultures were serially diluted 5-fold, and 10 muL of each dilution was spotted onto SD plates containing either glucose or galactose. Plates were incubated at 30 C for 2 days and photographed. Yeast cell lysates were prepared for immunoblotting according to established protocols.

passages.text: RT-qPCR

Total RNA was extracted from yeast cells using TRIzol Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) combined with acid-washed glass beads for mechanical lysis. cDNA was synthesized using the 5X All-In-One RT MasterMix (Abm). Quantitative PCR was performed using BlasTaq 2X qPCR MasterMix (Abm). Relative mRNA levels of RHO5 were calculated using the 2-DeltaDeltaCt method, with PGK1 serving as the internal reference control.
Immunoprecipitation and GST pull-down

HEK293T cells were transiently transfected with relevant plasmids. 24 h post-transfection, cells were harvested by washing once with ice-cold PBS and collected by centrifugation at 500 x g for 5 minutes at 4 C. Cell pellets were resuspended and lysed in ice-cold RIPA buffer supplemented with a protease inhibitor (Sigma) on ice for 10 minutes with occasional vortexing. Cell lysates were then clarified by centrifugation at 14,000 x g for 10 minutes at 4 C. The resulting supernatant was collected. For immunoprecipitation, the resulting supernatant was incubated with 10 microL slurry of anti-HA, anti-Flag, or anti-GFP agarose beads (AlpalifeBio) overnight at 4 C with gentle end-over-end rotation. Following incubation, the beads were washed 3 times with ice-cold RIPA buffer. Bound proteins were eluted from the beads by adding 30 microL of 1 x SDS-PAGE loading buffer and boiling at 95 C for 5 minutes. Eluted samples, along with input controls (40 microL of the initial lysate), were resolved by SDS-PAGE.

For the pull-down assay, 50 microg of purified GST-fusion protein was pre-incubated with 100 microL slurry of Glutathione High Capacity Magnetic Agarose Beads (Sigma) for 2 h at 4 C with gentle rotation to allow binding. After incubation, the beads were washed 3 times to remove unbound GST protein. Subsequently, the GST-protein-bound beads were incubated with the prey protein source. For the direct interaction assay shown in Fig 2D, a co-expression strategy was used to circumvent challenges with His6-SidG purification. Lysate from E. coli co-expressing GST-Rac1 and His6-SidG was incubated with glutathione beads overnight at 4 C. Finally, bound proteins were eluted by adding 30 microL of 1 x SDS-PAGE loading buffer and boiling at 95 C for 5 minutes. Eluted samples were analyzed by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting.

For the interaction assay between SidG and individual Arp2/3 subunits, a lysate-based co-immunoprecipitation strategy was employed. Bacterial lysates were prepared using bacterial active protein extraction reagent (Beyotime). To ensure detection of potential interactions independent of Rac1-mediated activation, bacterial lysates expressing GST-SidG were mixed with those expressing the Rac1-independent mutant GST-SidG1-797 to serve as the bait pool. This mixture was incubated with lysates containing individual His-Flag-tagged Arp2/3 subunits or His-Flag-Rac1. Immunoprecipitation was performed using Anti-Flag Affinity Gel (Sigma) at 4 C for 4 h. After washing three times with lysis buffer, bound proteins were eluted and analyzed by immunoblotting.
Antibodies and immunoblotting

For immunoblotting analysis, protein samples were resolved by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (Pall Life Sciences). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat dry milk in PBS containing 0.05% Tween-20 (PBS-T) for 1 h at room temperature. Subsequently, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 C with primary antibodies. Following washes with PBS-T, membranes were incubated with appropriate infrared dye-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. After final washes in PBS-T, membranes were imaged and fluorescence signals were acquired using the Odyssey CLx Infrared Imaging System (LI-COR Biosciences). A detailed list of primary antibodies and their working dilutions used in this study is provided in S4 Table.
Rac1 activation assay

Rac1 activation was assessed using a GST-PBD pull-down assay. Briefly, HEK293T cells were transfected with either HA-Rac1 or GFP-SidG, GFP-SidGH57A mutant, or the GFP control. After 24 h, cells were harvested and lysed separately in ice-cold RIPA buffer. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000 x g for 10 min at 4 C. Subsequently, lysates containing HA-Rac1 were combined with lysates containing either GFP-SidG, GFP-SidGH57A mutant, or the GFP control, and incubated at 37 C for 1 h. Supernatants were incubated with purified GST-PAK1 PBD immobilized on glutathione resin for 40 minutes at 4 C with gentle mixing. The beads were washed three times with RIPA buffer, and bound proteins (activated Rac1) were eluted by boiling in SDS sample loading buffer. Eluted proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and detected by Western blot analysis.
Random mutagenesis by hydroxylamine

Random mutagenesis of the p425GPD-SidG plasmid was performed by hydroxylamine treatment, following a previously described protocol. In brief, 5 microg of plasmid DNA was incubated in a 100 microL reaction mixture containing 0.5 M hydroxylamine, 5 mM Tris-HCl (pH 6.0), and 0.5 mM Na2-EDTA. The reaction was carried out for 10 h at 37 C or alternatively for 1 h at 65 C. Following the incubation, the mutagenized DNA product was recovered and transformed into the W303 for subsequent analysis.
Immunofluorescence staining

HeLa or HEK293 cells were seeded onto sterile glass coverslips placed in 24-well, transfected with the indicated plasmids. At 24 h post-transfection, cells were washed once with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 30 minutes at room temperature (RT). Following fixation, cells were permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 minutes, then blocked with 4% goat serum (Beyotime) for 30 minutes at RT. Cells were incubated with primary antibodies for 1 h at RT or overnight at 4 C. After washing with PBST, cells were incubated for 1 h at RT (protected from light) with appropriate secondary antibodies: Texas Red-conjugated goat anti-Mouse IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, T6390, 1:500) or Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated Goat anti-Rabbit IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A-11008, 1:500). Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI or Hoechst 33342 (Beyotime, C1022, 1:10000). Images were acquired on an Olympus FV3000 confocal microscope.
Differential staining for invasion kinetics

To distinguish between extracellular and intracellular bacteria during the early stages of infection (0-2 h), a differential staining protocol was employed. Cells were infected with the indicated L. pneumophila strains and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at the indicated time points. To label extracellular bacteria, cells were incubated with a rat anti-L. pneumophila antibody, followed by staining with an Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated anti-rat secondary antibody (Abcam) prior to permeabilization. Subsequently, cells were permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100. Total bacteria (both extracellular and intracellular) were then detected by incubation with a rabbit anti-L. pneumophila antibody, followed by an Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Abcam).
Infection and replication assays

For intracellular replication assays, BMDMs (4 x 105 cells/well) or Dictyostelium discoideum (5 x 105 cells/well) were seeded into 24-well plates and allowed to adhere overnight. L. pneumophila strains were used to infect the host cells at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.05 for BMDMs (incubated at 37 C) or 0.1 for D. discoideum (incubated at 25 C). After 2 h of infection, extracellular bacteria were removed by washing wells three times with PBS and incubating the cells with medium containing 100 microg/mL gentamicin for 1 h to kill any remaining extracellular bacteria. Cells were collected and lysed using 0.02% saponin in sterile PBS at the indicated time points. Lysates were serially diluted and plated onto CYE agar plates. Colony Forming Units (CFUs) were enumerated after incubation at 37 C for 3-4 days to determine intracellular bacterial numbers.

For immunofluorescence analysis of infected cells, HEK293 cells were seeded onto sterile glass coverslips placed in 24-well plates. Cells were co-transfected with plasmids encoding GFP-Rac1/ArpC3 along with plasmid pJC119R, which express FCgammaRII. At 24 h post-transfection, bacteria were opsonized with anti-L. pneumophila antibody for 30 min at 37 C prior to infecting the cells at an MOI of 20. Following infection, cells were processed for immunofluorescence as described in the 'Immunofluorescence Staining' section.

To quantify bacterial invasion, RAW 264.7 cells were seeded into 24-well plates at a density of 4 x 105 cells/well and allowed to adhere overnight. L. pneumophila strains, grown to post-exponential phase, were used to infect the cells at an MOI of 100. The infection was synchronized by centrifuging the plates at 1,000 x g for 5 min. After a 10-minute incubation at 37 C, cells were washed and treated with gentamicin as described above to eliminate extracellular bacteria. The number of invaded bacteria was then determined by enumerating CFUs following cell lysis, as described for the intracellular replication assay.
Mass spectrometry analysis

To identify proteins interacting with SidG constructs, immunoprecipitated samples were resolved by SDS-PAGE. Protein bands were visualized by Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining, excised from the gel, and subjected to in-gel digestion with trypsin. The resulting peptide mixtures were analyzed by LC-MS/MS using an Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Wound healing assay

The wound healing assay was performed following previously described methods. Briefly, HEK293 or RAW 264.7 cells were seeded into 6-well plates and allowed to reach approximately 90% confluence, forming a cell monolayer. A linear scratch, simulating a wound, was created in the center of the monolayer using a sterile 200 microL pipette tip. Detached cells and debris were then removed by gently washing the plates with serum-free medium. Following the wash, the cells were incubated at 37 C. Images of the scratch area, representing the initial wound width (2 h time point), were captured using an Olympus IX-83 microscope after 2 h of incubation. The cells were subsequently incubated for an additional 22 h. After the 24 h incubation period, images of the same scratch areas were acquired again to measure the final wound width (24 h time point). Wound healing was quantified using ImageJ software (https://imagej.net/ij/). The cell-free gap width was measured at multiple points along each scratch at both the 2 h (initial width) and 24 h (final width) time points. The percentage of wound closure was calculated using the following formula: % Wound Closure = [(Initial Width - Final Width)/ Initial Width] x 100.
Cell viability assay

HEK293T cells were seeded in 96-well plates and transfected with the indicated plasmids. At 24 h post-transfection, 10 microL of Cell Counting Kit-8 solution (APExBIO) was added to each well containing 100 microL of medium. The plates were incubated at 37 C for 1-2 h, and the absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a multimode microplate reader (BioTek Synergy H1).
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)

HEK293T cells were cultured on sterile glass coverslips and transfected with plasmids encoding either GFP or GFP-SidG. Following transfection, cells were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde at room temperature. After washing three times with PBS, samples were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series (30%, 50%, 70%, 80%, 90%, 95%, and 100% ethanol, 10 min each step). Samples were then allowed to air dry completely for at least 2 h. Dried coverslips were mounted onto aluminum stubs using conductive adhesive and sputter-coated with gold-palladium (Au-Pd). Cell surface morphology was examined using a Hitachi S-4800 scanning electron microscope at an accelerating voltage of 10 kV.
Bioinformatics and structure prediction

Multiple sequence alignments, comparing SidG with homologs from different Legionella species, and relevant host proteins were generated using the CLUSTALW algorithm (https://www.genome.jp/tools-bin/clustalw). Conserved residues and motifs, including the Cys-His-Asp motif, were visualized and annotated using GeneDoc. HMMER (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/hmmer/search/phmmer) was used with profile Hidden Markov Models to analyze SidG for evolutionary sequence conservation and identify key conserved sequence features.

AlphaFold (https://alphafoldserver.com/) was used to generate in silico predictions of structural coordinates for SidG, its homologs, Rac1, and Arp2/3 complex components. The predicted three-dimensional structures were then visualized, superimposed, and examined using PyMOL (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 2.5.5 Schrodinger, LLC.). Putative protein-protein interaction interfaces, particularly between SidG and Rac1, were investigated based on the predicted structures. Detailed analysis of potential interfacial residues, including predicted hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts, was performed and visualized in two dimensions using LigPlot+ v.2.2. Schematic diagrams summarizing interaction contacts and protein secondary structure topology were generated using PDBsum (www.ebi.ac.uk/thornton-srv/databases/pdbsum/).
Statistical analyses

Statistical significance between two groups was determined using the unpaired two-tailed Student's t-test, while one-way ANOVA was used for multiple group comparisons. p-values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA).

passages.text: Transcriptomic analysis of Atractylodes lancea (Thunb.) DC under methyl jasmonate induction reveals the terpene synthase genes related to sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis
Background

Methyl jasmonate (MeJA) serves as a potent elicitor of plant specialized metabolism, including terpenoid biosynthesis. The medicinal rhizome of Atractylodes lancea, renowned in traditional Chinese medicine, synthesizes pharmaceutically active sesquiterpenoids responsible for its therapeutic efficacy against rheumatic diseases, digestive disorders, and night blindness. However, the molecular understanding of MeJA-mediated sesquiterpene biosynthesis in A. lancea is not clear. Thus, it is important to explore the molecular mechanism and genes involved in sesquiterpene biosynthesis pathway underlying the response of A. lancea to MeJA.
Results

Combining MeJA elicitation with transcriptome profiling, we identified 25 sesqui-terpenoids synthase (AlTPS) gene in A. lancea via KEGG enrichment analysis and conserved motif analysis. Correlation analysis between DEGs and sesquiterpenoid accumulation, coupled with phylogenetic assessment, identified AlTPS7 and AlTPS8 as prime candidates, showing close homology to the characterized beta-eudesmol synthase ZmZSS2. Functional characterization revealed that AlTPS8 could catalyze the conversion of FPP into beta-caryophyllene, with a small amount of alpha-caryophyllene as a byproduct, whereas AlTPS7 was enzymatically inactive. Notably, quantitative analysis revealed AlTPS8's superior catalytic efficiency, producing beta-caryophyllene at 3.14-fold higher titers (0.36 +- 0.04 mg/L) than our previously characterized AlTPS6*, as quantified by in vivo product accumulation. Structural modeling and mutagenesis analyses revealed four key divergent residues (ALA398, SER402, THR449, ASN525) in AlTPS6* that regulate functional divergence, with the substitution of ASN525 to ASP being critical for enhancing catalytic efficiency.
Conclusions
These results provide mechanistic insights into MeJA-responsive sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis in A. lancea and a genetic toolkit for metabolic engineering of high-value medicinal terpenoids.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12864-026-12612-2.
Background

Atractylodes lancea (Thunb.) DC., a perennial herb of the Asteraceae family, is one of the primary botanical sources of the traditional Chinese medicine "Cangzhu". This pharmacologically important plant has garnered increasing attention in modern therapeutics, particularly for its demonstrated efficacy against COVID-19. Modern pharmacological studies have unveiled that A. lancea exhibits a wide range of pharmacological effects, including anti-ulcerogenic, gastrointestinal motility regulation, anti-hypoxic, antiviral, hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, central nervous system inhibitory, anticancer, hypoglycemic. The therapeutic potential of A. lancea is intricately linked to its complex secondary metabolome, within which sesquiterpenoids (such as atractylone, beta-eudesmol, and hinesol) and polyacetylenes emerge as the predominant bioactive constituents. These compounds display remarkable pharmacological diversity, encompassing anti-obesity, anti-hypoxic and antitumor activities, among others. The growing medicinal demand for A. lancea has intensified research into its terpenoid biosynthesis pathways, particularly the enzymatic mechanisms governing structural diversity.

Terpenoid biosynthesis in plants follows the conserved three-stage pathway: (i) precursor generation via the plastidial MEP and cytosolic MVA pathways producing Isopentenyl Pyrophosphate (IPP)/ Dimethylallyl Pyrophosphate (DMAPP); (ii) backbone formation through terpene synthases (TPSs)-the critical rate-limiting step converting Geranyl Pyrophosphate (GPP)/ Farnesyl Pyrophosphate (FPP)/ Geranylgeranyl Pyrophosphate (GGPP) to basic skeletons; and (iii) structural diversification by cytochrome P450s and glycosyltransferases. While TPSs have been characterized in various medicinal plants, including Cymbidium faberi and Aquilaria sinensis, and have been shown to produce compounds such as beta-myrcene, limonene, and germacrene D. Only a subset of AlTPSs has been functionally annotated, leaving significant gaps in understanding sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis regulation.

Methyl jasmonate (MeJA), a plant stress hormone first isolated from Jasminum grandiflorum, has emerged as a powerful elicitor of secondary metabolism. Beyond its established role in stress response modulation, MeJA significantly enhances production of valuable metabolites like physalins and plumbagin. However, the intricacies of MeJA affect changes in the transcriptome of terpenoid biosynthesis genes remain barely clarified, despite available transcriptomes of different tissues and geographical variants.

Here, we present the first comprehensive investigation of MeJA-induced transcriptional reprogramming in A. lancea. Combining Illumina-based transcriptomics with targeted metabolite profiling, we identified key sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis genes responsive to MeJA treatment. We further characterized two AlTPSs (AlTPS7 and AlTPS8) through heterologous expression. Our findings revealed that while AlTPS8 exhibits beta-caryophyllene synthase activity and produces a small amount of alpha-caryophyllene, AlTPS7 appears non-functional, suggesting divergent evolutionary trajectories within this gene family. Additionally, we discovered that AlTPS8 has better catalytic efficiency, generating beta-caryophyllene at 3.14 times higher levels than the previously studied AlTPS6*, which may be attributed to the key active site (Asp525) identified by molecular docking and site-directed mutagenesis. Our findings not only elucidate the molecular basis of MeJA-enhanced sesquiterpenoid production but also provide genetic tools for metabolic engineering of this pharmacologically important species.
Materials and methods
Plant materials and MeJA treatment

The seeds of A. lancea used in this study were collected from private lands near Zhanhe Reservoir in Yingshan County, Huanggang City, Hubei Province, China (29 36.32'N, 109 15.98'E). Then, they were surface-sterilized and germinated on Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with 2.0 mg/L 6-benzylaminopurine (6-BA) and 0.2 mg/L alpha-naphthaleneacetic acid (NAA). Seedlings were incubated in a growth chamber at 25 C, and under a 16 h light/8 h dark photoperiod. After two months of growth, uniformly developed seedlings of A. lancea were selected and transferred into the MS liquid medium with a final concentration of 200 microM MeJA. Control samples were maintained in MeJA-free medium. Subsequently, the samples were collected at 6 h, 12 h, 24 h, and 72 h, respectively, the untreated samples were used as the control group (CK). Treated samples were collected at 6, 12, 24, and 72 h post-induction, then rinsed three times with sterile water, blotted dry with sterile filter paper, immediately flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80  C until analysis. Three replicates were prepared for each group, with each replicate containing three plant samples.
Sesquiterpenoid profiling by GC-MS

The whole seedlings of A. lancea treated by MeJA described in the "Plant materials and MeJA treatment" section were freeze-dried for 48 h and homogenized to a fine powder. For each extraction, 0.3 g of dried material was subjected to ultrasonic-assisted extraction with 3 mL n-hexane for 2 h at 25  C. The extracts were centrifuged at 12,000 x g for 10 min, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 mum filter membrane prior to analysis.

Sesquiterpenoid analysis was performed on a gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS QP 2010 Ultra, Agilent), equipped with an 19091 S-433HP-5ms capillary column (30 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 mum). High-purity helium gas (> 99.999%) served as the carrier gas, with the flow rate of carrier gas helium at 1 mL/min. 1 microL of each sample aliquot was injected in the splitless mode at 280 C. The temperature program set as follows: the initial temperature of 60 C, increased to 90 C at a rate of 2 C/min, a further raised to 180 C at 5 C/min for 5 min, then raised to 260 C at 5 C/min, and a final hold for 5 min. Additional parameters included an inlet temperature of 280 C, an electron ionization source operating at 200 C, and a quadrupole temperature maintained at 150 C. Full MS SCAN mode was selected within an m/z range of 20~300.

The quantification of four key bioactive components (atractylodin, beta-eudesmol, hinesol, and atractylon) was achieved using the external standard method via GC-MS. Briefly, the four reference standards were individually separated on an 19091 S-433HP-5ms capillary column under optimized and consistent GC-MS conditions, and the concentration of each target component in the samples was calculated by interpolating its measured peak area into the pre-constructed calibration curve of the corresponding reference standard.
Total RNA extraction, library construction, and transcriptome sequencing

Three independent biological replicates were sequenced for each group (0 h, 12 h, and 72 h). The total RNA was extracted from each sample using a Plant RNA Kit (Simgen, China) following the manufacturer's instructions. RNA integrity was verified by agarose gel electrophoresis, while concentration and purity were determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (A260/A280 ratio > 1.8) and Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer with RNA HS Assay Kit. RNA-seq libraries were prepared using the NEB Next Ultra II RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina. Briefly, poly(A)+ mRNA was enriched using oligo(dT) magnetic beads and fragmented. First-strand cDNA was synthesized using random hexamer primers and M-MuLV Reverse Transcriptase, followed by second-strand synthesis. After end repair was performed and the cDNA fragments were enriched by PCR, the products were purified and circularized to obtain the final library. The DNBSEQ platform was utilized to conduct transcriptome sequencing. The high-quality clean reads were obtained from raw reads by removing reads containing adapters, low-quality reads (including reads with a removal ratio of N greater than 5% and more than 50% nucleotides with Qphred <= 5) and reads with a length less than 30 bp. The clean reads were aligned with the reference genome using STAR (v2.7.9a).
Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) analysis and functional annotation

DEGs analysis was performed to identify transcriptional responses to MeJA treatment across different time points. Gene expression levels were quantified as fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM) and normalized using the DESeq2 package (v1.26.0). Genes meeting the following criteria were considered differentially expressed: false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05, llog2 fold changel > 1, and adjusted p-value < 0.05. Then, GO (Gene Ontology) and KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) enrichment analysis were performed using cluster Profiler R package (v3.14.3) to gain insights into the functional characteristics of these DEGs. Heatmaps of DEGs were analyzed using genecloud website.
Verification of RT-qPCR analysis

To validate the RNA-seq results, the real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) was performed on 12 randomly selected DEGs involved in the terpenoid biosynthesis pathways in A. lancea. The glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) gene served as the internal control. Primers for the target DEGs were designed using Primer (v6.0) software (Premier, Canada) (Table S1). The RT-qPCR was performed in a 20 microL reaction volume containing 1 microL of cDNA template (500 ng/microL), 0.4 microL of each forward/reverse primer (10 microM), 10 microL of BrightCycle Universal SYBR Green qPCR Mix with UDG (Abclonal, Wuhan, China), and 8.2 microL ddH2O. The reactions were carried out on an iCycler iQ Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, USA). Amplification reactions were performed according to the following program: 37 C for 2 min, 95 C for 3 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95 C for 5 s, 60 C for 30 s. The expression levels were calculated using the 2-DeltaDeltaCt method with three replicates.
Cloning the full-length cDNA of candidate AlTPSs

Based on the sequences obtained from the genomic data, the full-length open reading frame (ORF) of candidate AlTPSs was cloned according to the manufacturer's instructions of 2x Phanta Flash Master Mix P510 (Vazyme, China). The primers used are listed in Table S1. PCR conditions were as follows: 98 C for 30 s, followed by 35 cycles of three steps (98 C for 10 s, 60 C for 5 s, 72 C for 10 s), then 72 C for 1 min. The PCR products were purified and cloned into the TOPO vector (TransGen Biotech, China) and positive clones were sequenced by Sangon Biotech (Wuhan, China).
Functional identification of candidate AlTPSs using in S. cerevisiae

The full-length open reading frame (ORF) of AlTPSs was cloned into the SpeI/NotI sites of the yeast expression vector pESC-URA respectively. The recombinant plasmid was transformed into S. cerevisiae THY19 competent cells (an FPP-overproducing strain) individually and selected on SD-Ura solid medium. Positive clones were inoculated into 5 mL of SD-Ura liquid medium and cultured overnight at 30 C with shaking at 200 rpm to serve as the seed culture. The seed culture was added to 20 mL of SD-Ura liquid medium and diluted until the optical density (OD) was approximately 0.2. Then, 2 mL of dodecane was added to the system for liquid sealing. After continuous fermentation at 30 C and with shaking at 200 rpm for 3 days, the liquid culture was centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 10 min. The upper organic layer after centrifugation was collected, and then subjected to GC-MS (Agilent 19091 S-433 HP-5ms) detection. Detecting conditions were as follows: the initial temperature of 100 C for 2 min, which increased to 200 C at a rate of 30 C/min and maintained at that temperature for 1 min, then raised to 260 C at 20 C/min for 1 min. Mass spectra were recorded in the mass range of m/z 20 ~ 300.
beta-Caryophyllene quantification was performed using a seven-point calibration curve, monitoring m/z 204.2 for quantification and 161.1 for confirmation.
Molecular Docking and site-directed mutagenesis of AlTPSs

In order to identify catalytic sites and infer enzyme-substrate binding conformations, molecular docking analysis was performed to evaluate the interaction between the target enzyme with the FPP small molecule ligand. The 3D chemical structure files in SDF of FPP was retrieved from PubChem compound database (PubChem CID: 445713, https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov), and then converted to PDB format by Open Babel GUI. For homology modeling of AlTPSs, we used the crystal structure of AF-A0A5N6NJV0-F1-model-v4 (SWISS-MODEL template library) as a template, which shares > 71% sequence coverage with the target proteins. Hydrogens were added to both ligands and receptors using AutoDock Tools (v1.5.7), followed by batch analysis of binding energies and sites by AutoDock Vina (v1.2.5). Pymol software (v3.1.3) was used to visualize ligand-receptor structures and analyze their interactions.

Site-directed mutagenesis was performed by using the pESC-URA-AlTPS6* vector as the template for amplification. Primers used for mutagenesis are listed in Table S1. The PCR products were digested with Dpn I enzyme at 37 C for 30 min, purified using a DNA purification kit (Simgen, China) and then transformed into DH5alpha competent cells (WeiDi, China). Then positive clones were sequenced by Sangon Biotech (Wuhan, China). The recombinant strains were further transformed into S. cerevisiae THY19 competent cells, and the expression of AlTPS6* mutant vectors was analyzed as described in the "Functional identification of candidate AlTPSs using in S. cerevisiae" section.
Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (v10.1.2).: catalytic efficiency was compared via T-test, and other data via one-way ANOVA, with three biological replicates per construct. All statistical procedures were performed rigorously to ensure the robustness and validity of the results.
Results
Determination of sesquiterpenoid accumulation in MeJA-treated A. lancea

GC-MS quantification revealed distinct temporal accumulation patterns for four medicinally important compounds in A. lancea seedlings following elicitation with 200 microM MeJA (Fig. 1). The standard curves of the four target compound standards used for quantification exhibited good linearity (R2 > 0.99), confirming the reliability and precision of the GC-MS quantification method (Fig. S1). Quantitative profiling demonstrated that beta-eudesmol exhibited the most rapid response, with significant elevation observed at 6 h post-treatment (P < 0.001), peaking at 12 h. The atractylodin and atractylon exhibited significant increases at 12 h (P < 0.05), while hinesol accumulation was delayed until 72 h (P < 0.001). Our findings indicate that exogenous application of MeJA can effectively promote the accumulation of sesquiterpenoids (including beta-eudesmol, hinesol, and atractylon) and also increased atractylodin levels in A. lancea.

Transcriptome sequencing and quality assessment

Our phytochemical analysis revealed that MeJA treatment significantly induced the accumulation of beta-eudesmol, atractylone, and atractylodin at 12 h (P < 0.05), with a delayed production peak observed for hinesol at 72 h (P < 0.01). Notably, only beta-eudesmol showed a significant increase at the early 6 h time point (P < 0.01), whereas the other three key compounds did not exhibit statistically significant accumulation at either 6 h or 24 h. Based on this distinct temporal accumulation pattern, we selected the 12 h and 72 h time points for comprehensive transcriptome sequencing to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Total RNA was extracted from A. lancea treated with 200 microM MeJA at three critical time points (0, 12, and 72 h) and subjected to transcriptome sequencing. After removing the low-quality data and the data containing the adaptor, a total of 35.3 Gb of clean data was obtained, and each library yielded at least 36,791,438 clean reads. The Q20 and Q30 percentages exceeded 96.821% and 92.487%, and the GC content ranged from 44.339% to 44.624%. Alignment of the clean data with the A. lancea genome produced alignment rates ranging from 91.73% to 92.61% (Table S2). And the mapping rates for all samples range from 91.71% to 92.63%, with a coefficient of variation (CV) of < 2% among replicates of the same time point. This low variability indicates consistent library quality and sequencing performance across biological replicates, validating the reliability of the RNA-seq data (Table S3). These results confirmed the high quality of the sequencing data, suitable for subsequent analyses.
DEGs identification across MeJA-induced transcriptome in A. lancea

To elucidate the molecular basis of MeJA-induced terpenoid biosynthesis, we performed differential gene expression analysis in A. lancea treated with 200 microM MeJA for 0, 12, and 72 h (Fig. 2). The total number of annotated genes is 81,612. The MeJA-12 h vs. CK comparison showed the most dramatic transcriptional changes, with 5,115 (6.27%) genes up-regulated and 6,902 (8.46%) down-regulated. In the MeJA-72 h vs. CK comparison, 3853 (4.72%) genes were up regulated and 5366 (6.58%) genes were down regulated. And 1727 (2.12%) up-regulated genes and 1190 (1.46%) down-regulated genes were identified in the MeJA-72 h vs. MeJA-12 h comparison. Venn diagrams serve as a powerful visual tool to show the number of shared and distinctive DEGs among different time points of MeJA induction. The Venn diagram demonstrated that 1034 (1.27%) genes showed differential expression across any two time points following MeJA induction, whereas 5117 (6.27%) genes had differential expression merely at a specific time point after MeJA induction.

Identification of candidate genes involved in sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis

Terpenoids are the most abundant compounds in A. lancea, responsible for its broad pharmacological properties. Our comprehensive KEGG pathway analysis identified genes participating in terpenoid backbone (ko00900), along with monoterpenoid (ko00902), diterpenoid (ko00904), and sesquiterpenoid and triterpenoid (ko00909). With the MVA pathway, we annotated 15 DEGs encoding core enzymes: 3 acetyl-CoA acetyltransferases (AACT), 2 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthases (HMGS), 7 HMG-CoA reductases (HMGR), 1 mevalonate kinase (MVK), 1 5-phosphomevalonate kinase (PMK), and 1 mevalonate-5-pyrophosphate decarboxylase (MVD). Strikingly, the vast majority of MVA pathway genes demonstrated significantly elevated expression levels following 12 h MeJA treatment compared to other time points, indicating jasmonate-mediated activation of sesquiterpenoid precursor biosynthesis. Parallel analysis revealed 6 genes in the MEP pathway, including 3 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate synthases (DXS), 1 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate reductoisomerase (DXR), 1 4-diphosphocytidyl-2-C-methyl-D-erythritol kinase (CMK), 1 2-C-Methyl-D-erythritol-2,4-cyclodiphosphate synthase (MDS). Downstream terpenoid biosynthesis involves critical transformations of IPP and DMAPP, which are converted to GPP and FPP by GPPS and FPPS. Our annotation identified 2 FPPS genes and 3 IDI genes. Notably, 25 sesqui-TPSs were associated with the sesquiterpenoid and triterpenoid biosynthesis pathway (ko00909). All these genes encode proteins that contain core conserved motifs specific to sesqui-TPSs, including the DDXXD and NSE/DTE motifs which are essential for FPP binding, which further validating their functional classification as sesqui-TPSs (Fig. S2). Following MeJA induction, 14 of these genes exhibited significant upregulation, displaying distinct temporal expression patterns. Specifically, 10 gene reached peak expression levels at 12 h post-induction, while 4 genes showed maximal induction at the 72 h time point. In contrast, 9 genes demonstrated consistent downregulation throughout the treatment period. Interestingly, 2 genes displayed a biphasic response pattern, characterized by initial downregulation followed by subsequent upregulation, suggesting complex regulatory mechanisms in sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis under jasmonate signaling (Fig. 4).

Screening and bioinformatics analysis of candidate AlTPSs for sesquiterpene biosynthesis pathway

To elucidate the molecular basis of sesquiterpene biosynthesis in A. lancea, we performed correlation analysis between the expression levels of 25 sesqui-AlTPSs and the contents of sesquiterpene component under MeJA treatment. As Fig. 6A shown that eight AlTPSs (AlTPS2-9) exhibited positive correlations with the sesquiterpenoid atractylone. Among these, six gene (AlTPS3, AlTPS5-9) also showed positive associations with beta-eudesmol, while AlTPS25 was positively correlated with the content of hinesol. These results revealed that these AlTPSs may play important roles in sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis in A. lancea. Phylogenetic reconstruction incorporating these eight candidates AlTPSs and functionally characterized TPS homologs from related species provided further mechanistic insights (Fig. 6B). The clustering of AlTPS7 and AlTPS8 with ZSS2, a known beta-eudesmol synthase from Zingiber zerumbet, suggesting functional relevance in sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis. This evolutionary relationship, combined with their co-expression patterns with beta-eudesmol accumulation, identifies AlTPS7 and AlTPS8 as prime candidates for mediating this pharmacologically important sesquiterpenoid pathway in A. lancea. Based on transcriptome data of A. lancea, we successfully cloned the open reading frames (ORFs) of two candidate sesquiterpene synthase genes, AlTPS7 (1569 bp, encoding 522 amino acids) and AlTPS8 (1653 bp, encoding 550 amino acids). The predicted tertiary structures of AlTPS7 and AlTPS8 are shown in Fig. 6C and D. Tertiary structure prediction using Swiss model identified AF-A0A5N6NJV0-F1-model-v4 as the highest-confidence model. Further, multiple sequences alignment identified conserved catalytic motifs essential for terpene synthase activity, including the metal-binding domains RXR, DDXXD, as well as NSE/DTE signatures in conserved catalytic motifs. Notably, while both AlTPS7 and AlTPS8 contained these core motifs, the RR(X)8 W signature characteristic of many sesquiterpene synthases was absent in AlTPS7 but present in AlTPS8 (Fig. 6E).

Heterologous expression and functional characterization of AlTPSs in S. cerevisiae

Through heterologous expression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we systematically characterized the catalytic properties of two candidate sesquiterpene synthases from A. lancea. GC-MS analysis revealed distinct product profiles: while AlTPS7 showed no detectable activity, AlTPS8 catalyzed the formation of a compound eluting at 4.5 min which was absent in the empty vector (Fig. 7A; Fig. S5). Comparative analysis with authentic standards and NIST database matching identified this product as beta-caryophyllene, confirmed by identical retention times (Fig. 7B) and characteristic mass spectral fragmentation patterns (Fig. 7E and G). Besides, by analogy with the authentic standard, AlTPS8 additionally produced alpha-caryophyllene (peak 2 at 4.64 min), demonstrating bifunctional activity in converting FPP to caryophyllene isomers (Fig. 7A, C, F and H). According to the previous research, AlTPS6* (* represent previously characterized synthase) also could catalyze FPP to beta-caryophyllene in vitro enzymatic reactions. According to both AlTPS6* and AlTPS8 produce the same product and the amino acid sequence similarity between AlTPS6* and AlTPS8 was 86.31% (Fig. 7A; Fig. S6), a quantitative analysis of their efficiency in generating beta-caryophyllene was further conducted. Quantitative analysis using a validated GC-MS calibration curve (y = 217,733.38x - 3,076.93; R2 = 0.9979, Fig. S7) revealed significant differences in catalytic efficiency between isoforms, with AlTPS8 generating 3.14-fold higher beta-caryophyllene yields than AlTPS6* (p < 0.0001, Fig. 7D). This pronounced functional divergence between the two closely related isoforms suggested important structural differences in their active site architecture or substrate binding kinetics.

Molecular Docking of the protein encoded by the AlTPS6* and AlTPS8

To elucidate the molecular basis for the observed differences in catalytic efficiency between AlTPS6* and AlTPS8, we performed comprehensive structural analyses. Molecular docking revealed both AlTPS6* and AlTPS8 maintained strong binding affinity for FPP, with calculated binding energies of -8.2 kcal/mol for AlTPS8 and - 8.0 kcal/mol for AlTPS6* (Fig. 8A and D). Detailed analysis of the protein-ligand interactions revealed distinct binding patterns: AlTPS6* formed five hydrogen bonds with FPP, primarily mediated by ARG264 and ASN525 (Fig. 8B), whereas AlTPS8 established three hydrogen bonds involving SER402, ASP447, and HIS452 (Fig. 8E). Comparative structural analysis within the 5 A active site radius identified four key divergent residues between the isoforms: ALA399, SER402, THR449, ASN525 in AlTPS6*, corresponding THR399, CYS402, SER449, ASP525 in AlTPS8 (Fig. 8C and F).

Key residues that affect the generation of products

To further investigate the amino acid sites responsible for the difference in catalytic efficiency, we mutated the key candidate residues selected from molecular docking on AlTPS6* one by one into the corresponding key residues on AlTPS8 (Fig. 8G). Subsequent site-directed mutagenesis studies demonstrated that the N525D substitution in AlTPS6* resulted in a 7.33-fold increase in beta-caryophyllene production (p < 0.0001), while analogous mutations at the other three candidate positions (A398T; S402C; T449S) showed no statistically significant effects on product yield (p > 0.05) (Fig. 8H). It is indicated that mutating ASN525 on AlTPS6* to ASP can enhance the catalytic efficiency of beta-caryophyllene, suggesting that the ASP residue may involve in governing the enzyme's cyclization activity.
Discussion

MeJA is a well-established phytohormonal elicitor that regulates the biosynthesis of plant specialized metabolites, including terpenoids, flavonoids and phenolics in medicinal plants. Preharvest MeJA application can increase the content of phenolic components in postharvest grape berries, like resveratrol and quercetin. Similarly, exogenous MeJA increased plumbagin and saponin levels in P.auriculata, and significantly induced the accumulation of physalins D and H (over 2-fold) in Cutleaf Groundcherry. As the largest group of secondary metabolites in plants, terpenoids which are the major bioactive components in A. lancea present high medicinal and industrial value. In this study, treatment with 200 microM MeJA differentially induced the accumulation of key bioactive sesquiterpenoids in A. lancea, including beta-eudesmol, hinesol, atractylone, and atractylodin.

Nowadays, transcriptome sequencing has been extensively employed to dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying MeJA-induced secondary metabolite biosynthesis in various medicinal plants, such as Carthamus tinctorius L, Forsythia suspensa, Camellia vietnamensis Huang, and Bupleurum chinense DC. However, the potential biosynthesis and regulatory mechanisms of terpenoid in A. lancea under exogenous MeJA remain largely elusive. Our transcriptomic profiling of MeJA-treated A. lancea revealed extensive transcriptional reprogramming, with 12,017 and 9,219 DEGs identified at 12 and 72 h post-treatment, respectively, compared to the control. This dynamic expression pattern : characterized by an acute transcriptional response followed by gradual stabilization : suggests a coordinated stress adaptation mechanism. Notably, this transcriptional behavior aligns with the observed accumulation peak of major sesquiterpenoid active compounds at 12 h.

To further elucidate how MeJA enhances active component accumulation, we performed functional annotation of DEGs for both time points. GO enrichment analysis highlighted significant involvement in defense response, lipid metabolic process carbohydrate, metabolic process, oxidoreductase activity, while KEGG analysis revealed predominant involvement in metabolic pathways, secondary metabolite biosynthesis, and plant-pathogen interactions. These findings collectively underscore the complex regulatory networks activated by MeJA in A. lancea. Besides, analysis of the transcriptome data also revealed that the expression levels of some key genes including AACT, HMGS, HMGR, MVK, PMK, MVD and TPS on the sesquiterpenoid pathway were upregulated after MeJA treatment. These results indicated that MeJA may regulate sesquiterpenoid content via transcriptional regulation of the biosynthetic pathway.

Sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis requires coordinated enzyme activities, primarily mediated by TPSs in conjunction with cytochrome P450 enzymes and other modifying enzymes. TPSs are essential for catalyzing the formation of terpenoids and serve as key drivers of the diversity of terpene hydrocarbon skeletons. The functional characterization of TPSs has been reported across diverse medicinal plants. AsTPS9 and AsTPS12 isolated from Aquilaria sinensis could produce a variety of terpenoids, including geraniol, citronellol, and limonene. In Cymbidium faberi, the level of geraniol, beta-myrcene and alpha-pinene is regulated by CfTPS18. Two TPSs, AkTPS1 and AkTPS2, have been isolated from Angelica keiskei, with AkTPS1 catalyzing the production germacrene D, and AkTPS2 producing germacrene B and smaller amounts of germacrene D. AmAOS from Artemisia maritima could cyclize FPP to 4-amorphen-11-ol. In Taiwania cryptomerioides, the content of alpha-gurjunene is related to Tc-Gur. ZzZSS2 could catalyze the formation of beta-eudesmol and five additional by-products in Zingiber zerumbet. Thus, in order to identify TPSs that involved in MeJA-induced sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis, we conducted comparative transcriptomics and identified 25 sesquiterpene synthase-like genes (sesqui-AlTPSs). Among these, eight exhibited a strong correlation with sesquiterpenoid accumulation, suggesting that these genes may contribute significantly to the accumulation of sesquiterpenoid. Phylogenetic analysis further prioritized AlTPS7 and AlTPS8 as putative sesquiterpenoid synthases due to their high homology with ZzZSS2, a characterized beta-eudesmol-producing enzyme in Zingiber zerumbet. This led us to hypothesize that both AlTPS7 and AlTPS8 might be involved in beta-eudesmol biosynthesis in A. lancea. However, heterologous functional characterization in S. cerevisia showed AlTPS8 could catalyze the conversion of FPP into beta-caryophyllene and trace alpha-caryophyllene, while AlTPS7 appears non-functional, and failed to produce beta-eudesmol.

To elucidate the underlying mechanistic basis, we performed structural analysis of these TPS proteins and identified three conserved motifs in their C-terminal domains: DDXXD, NSE/DTE, and RXR. The aspartate-rich DDXXD motif, situated at the entrance of the active site, chelates divalent metal ions and binds the diphosphate group of the substrate to ensure proper positioning. Upon entry of FPP into the hydrophobic active site, the DDXXD and the opposing NSE/DTE motif cooperatively coordinate three divalent metal ions to form a metal coordination cluster. This cluster interacts with the diphosphate group of FPP, leading to active site closure. The resulting farnesyl cation then undergoes cyclization and rearrangement within the enclosed cavity, ultimately forming sesquiterpene or alcohol products via deprotonation or water quenching. Notably, the NSE/DTE motif sequences between AlTPS8 and ZzZSS2 are not fully conserved compared to ZzZSS2, which may explain their divergent product profiles despite 72.53% sequence identity. A similar functional divergence has been observed between AcTPS1 and CiTPS1, which cluster together phylogenetically yet produce germacrene D and alpha-pinene, respectively. Furthermore, analogous to the case described here, ZcTPS1:which lacks the RR(X8)W motif:is catalytically inactive, while ZcTPS2, containing this motif, functions as a beta-ocimene synthase. The RR(X8)W motif is known to shield carbocation intermediates from solvent access during catalysis, thereby maintaining the hydrophobic environment essential for cyclization and rearrangement. Loss of this motif may lead to premature reaction termination and failure to generate the intended product. Importantly, AlTPS7 also lacks the RR(X8)W motif, leading us to hypothesize that this structural deficiency may be responsible for its loss of enzymatic activity.

Moreover, AlTPS8 exhibited catalytic activity consistent with that of AlTPS6*, previously amplified by our research group. Comparison of their catalytic efficiencies revealed that AlTPS8 produced 0.36 mg/L beta-caryophyllene, 3.14-fold higher than AlTPS6*. Interestingly, AlTPS8 and AlTPS6* share high sequence similarity, their catalytic efficiencies differ substantially. Previous study exhibited that different amino acid side chain groups can influence the transfer direction of carbocation intermediates or the ability of enzymes to capture solvent molecules. A single amino acid substitution in the active site of plant terpene synthases can affect product specificity or yield. For example, two mutants of ZmEDS from Zea mays (ZmEDS: I279G and ZmEDS: V306A) can correspondingly produce substantial amounts of 3-epi-cryptomeridiol and 2,3-epi-cryptomeridiol. In Curcuma wenyujin, mutating the aliphatic amino acids Leu295 and Leu298 in helix D of the CwTPS5 to alanine resulted in a decrease in olefin production. Structural analysis identified four critical sites (ALA399, SER402, THR449, ASN525 in AlTPS6*, corresponding THR399, CYS402, SER449, ASP525 in AlTPS8) that may govern functional divergence. Future, site-directed mutagenesis studies demonstrated that the N525D substitution in AlTPS6* resulted in a 7.33-fold increase in beta-caryophyllene production, indicating that replacing uncharged asparagine with negatively charged aspartate may stabilize carbocation intermediates through electrostatic complementarity, thereby lowering the energy barrier and increasing product yield.

beta-Caryophyllene, a sesquiterpenoid, holds considerable potential in pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, cosmetic, and chemical industries. These findings highlight AlTPS8's potential for metabolic engineering to optimize sesquiterpenoid production for pharmaceutical and industrial applications. Collectively, our findings not only advance the understanding of sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis in A. lancea but also establish a framework for optimizing high-value terpenoid production through enzyme engineering and synthetic biology approaches.
Conclusion

Our study establishes that MeJA elicitation enhances the accumulation of pharmacologically active sesquiterpenoids in A. lancea, while multi-omics integration unravels the transcriptional circuitry governing MeJA-induced terpenoid biosynthesis. transcriptome profiling identified 24,153 MeJA-responsive DEGs (10,695 upregulated; 13,458 downregulated), with functional enrichment revealing coordinated activation of defense responses, lipid/carbohydrate metabolism, and secondary metabolite biosynthesis pathways.

Among the DEGs, we identified 25 sesquiterpene synthase-like genes (AlTPSs), eight of which exhibited strong correlations with sesquiterpenoid accumulation. Phylogenetic and functional characterization prioritized AlTPS7 and AlTPS8, homologs of the previously characterized beta-eudesmol synthase ZzZSS2. Heterologous expression in S. cerevisiae confirmed that AlTPS8 catalyzes the conversion of FPP into beta-caryophyllene and trace alpha-caryophyllene. Notably, AlTPS8 exhibited a 3.14-fold increase in producing beta-caryophyllene compared with our previously characterized AlTPS6*. Four key sites were selected between AlTPS6* and AlTPS8 from structural modeling and mutagenesis analyses, with the N525D mutation (AlTPS6*: ASN525 to ASP) exhibiting superior catalytic efficiency. The N525D substitution was further validated as a key determinant of beta-caryophyllene productivity, indicating that the ASP residue is involved in the enzyme's cyclization activity and offering a strategic target for enzyme engineering. Collectively, this work elucidates the regulatory role of MeJA in sesquiterpenoid biosynthesis in A. lancea and identifies AlTPS8 as a high-efficiency-caryophyllene synthase. These findings not only advance our understanding of terpenoid biosynthesis in A. lancea, but also provide a genetic toolkit for metabolic engineering to optimize the production of pharmaceutically valuable sesquiterpenoids.
