passages.text: Practical and clinical significance of the pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) undermines clinical care. Thus, ensuring appropriate antimicrobial therapy is crucial in global and national AMR countermeasures. This narrative review aimed to summarize pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship interventions in Japan and discuss their practical and clinical significance across inpatient, outpatient, and community settings. In inpatient care, antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs), usually embedded within antimicrobial stewardship teams and supported by national policies and reimbursement incentives, have consistently reduced broad-spectrum antibiotic use (e.g., carbapenems). ASPs improve microbiological indicators such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa susceptibility while maintaining patient safety. The evidence of ASP efficiency spans large tertiary hospitals that consider post-prescription review with feedback and expanded prospective audit-and-feedback. In addition, small-to-medium hospitals that adopt pharmacist-led programs have demonstrated improved key process measures (culture acquisition, de-escalation, and duration of therapy), as well as optimized clinical outcomes in selected high-risk subgroups. Given that outpatient oral antibiotics account for a substantial proportion of total consumption, ASPs are increasingly being recognized as an essential approach. Reported pharmacist-led interventions include monitoring and feedback to high-prescription departments, regimen optimization based on susceptibility data, and dental outpatient programs that shift prescriptions from third-generation cephalosporins toward guideline-recommended penicillins. At the community level, regional educational outreach with surveillance feedback and peer-comparison approaches, as well as community pharmacy-based prescription optimization, have demonstrated meaningful shifts toward narrower-spectrum agents. Pharmacist-led ASPs in Japan have largely benefitted inpatients, whereas outpatient and community stewardship remains an essential frontier requiring enhanced implementation and rigorous assessment of patient-centered outcomes.
Background

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens the foundation of clinical care and jeopardizes the long-term viability of global public health strategies against infectious diseases. Appropriate antimicrobial therapy is essential for the prevention and treatment of infections, safeguarding patients from life-threatening conditions and enabling safe high-risk interventions, such as surgical procedures and cancer chemotherapy. However, the common and inappropriate use of antimicrobials in healthcare and agriculture has escalated the threats, causing a global hazard. With only a few new antibiotics under development, the options for future treatment are rapidly diminishing. The absence of coordinated and urgent global action could lead to a post-antibiotic era, where once-manageable infections could regain a deadly status. If effective and timely action against AMR remains lacking, by 2050, AMR could cause approximately 10 million deaths annually and result in major economic losses and social instability owing to reduced workforce productivity. The World Health Organization (WHO) has proposed a five-part framework to combat AMR, which is aimed at preventing these threats: "Investing in new medicines, diagnostic tools, vaccines and other interventions," "Improving the awareness and understanding of AMR through effective communication, education, and training," "Optimizing the use of antimicrobial medicines in human and animal health," "Reducing the incidence of infection through effective sanitation, hygiene and infection prevention measures, including vaccines," and "Strengthening the knowledge and evidence base through surveillance and research.". Among these, the appropriate use of antimicrobials is a critical concern for physicians, pharmacists, and other healthcare professionals in routine clinical practice; thus, supporting guidelines have been issued in Japan. In particular, a growing body of evidence has reported the outcomes of pharmacist-led stewardship activities, highlighting stewardship as an area requiring a significant contribution of pharmacists. Japan has generated considerable practical and clinical evidence to promote the appropriate use of antimicrobial agents. Therefore, this review aims to synthesize the available evidence on pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship in Japan. Furthermore, we have conducted research to generate clinical evidence in anaerobic infections, practical evidence in support activities for the antimicrobial stewardship by pharmacists, and practical evidence for the appropriate use of voriconazole and related topics. Based on previous reports, this review provides an overview of pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship interventions in Japan, with a particular focus on clarifying their clinical significance.
Pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship for inpatients

In Japan, antimicrobial stewardship has been reinforced through national AMR policy and reimbursement incentives that encourage hospitals to formalize antimicrobial stewardship teams (ASTs), where pharmacists are expected to play a central role. Several studies have reported pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship interventions for hospitalized patients. In the subsequent sections, we will discuss the clinical implications of these interventions according to hospital bed capacity.
Large-sized hospitals

Akazawa et al. evaluated an 8-year stepwise stewardship program in a tertiary hospital using interrupted time-series (ITS) analyses across three phases, namely consultation, monitoring with e-mail feedback, and post-prescription review and feedback (PPRF), which were led by infectious diseases (ID) physicians and pharmacists. The day of therapy (DOT) of carbapenems per 100 patient-days decreased across phases (median monthly 5.46   3.69   2.78), and the PPRF phase produced a sustained reduction without clear evidence of "squeezing the balloon" toward other broad agents. In Japan, differences in stewardship staffing and institutional support (including reimbursement-driven resources) may influence implementation and outcomes, underscoring the significance of presenting institutional experience. We examined whether the full-time equivalent (FTE) of an ID pharmacist influences PPRF effectiveness. After the introduction of an antimicrobial stewardship reimbursement fee, the ID pharmacist FTE increased from 0.34 to 0.63, broad-spectrum DOT decreased, and the susceptibility of Pseudomonas aeruginosa improved for meropenem and levofloxacin, supporting pharmacist capacity as an implementation lever. In addition, another multicenter investigation demonstrated that institutions with sufficient FTE staffing dedicated to antimicrobial stewardship activities showed a statistically significant reduction trend in the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Ohashi et al. expanded pharmacist-led prospective audit and feedback (PAF) from selected antibiotics to all injectable antibiotics. The mortality rate was unchanged; however, Intravenous antibiotic duration shortened, de-escalation and appropriate dosing improved, and the methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) to total S. aureus ratio decreased. Their subsequent 8-year evaluation demonstrated sustained improvements, including declining MRSA proportions, improved P. aeruginosa susceptibility (meropenem and levofloxacin), reduced therapy duration from 2017 onward, and reduced proportion of patients receiving prolonged IV therapy. Okada et al. assessed pharmacist-driven PAF for bloodstream infection using ITS analysis and found that de-escalation increased by 44% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 30-58), and DOT decreased for carbapenems and piperacillin/tazobactam (-16 and - 15 per 100 patient-days, respectively), without worse 30-day mortality.

Focused bundles are an efficient approach. Komatsu et al. evaluated a carbapenem program with reduced broad-spectrum use and maintained P. aeruginosa susceptibility. Suzuki et al. used an ITS design to assess an AST PPRF strategy focusing on carbapenem de-escalation; carbapenem DOT decreased (median, 33.2-15.3) in all departments except for the hematology Sect. These reports imply that pharmacist-led ASPs in large hospitals effectively reduce the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics such as carbapenems and improve susceptibility rates for pathogens, including P. aeruginosa.
Small- and medium-sized hospitals

Several studies have reported favorable outcomes for pharmacist-led ASPs even in small- and medium-sized hospitals. In a 126-bed community hospital, Nakamura et al. emphasized the significance of close communication among post-prescription audit pharmacists, ward pharmacists, and the ASTs. Implementation increased recommendations (10.4-21.1%), improved culture ordering (56.3-73.3%), increased de-escalation (10.2-30.8%), and reduced carbapenem use without worsening 30-day mortality. Furthermore, Nakano et al. conducted a pragmatic quasi-experimental study of a pharmacist-led ASP in a 260-bed secondary-care hospital (without ID physicians or an in-house microbiology laboratory) using PAF plus a pre-registration system for carbapenems. After implementation, carbapenem use significantly decreased (DOT, incidence rate ratio (IRR) = 0.53 [95% CI: 0.33-0.81]), along with overall spectrum breadth for injectable antimicrobials (days of antibiotic spectrum coverage, IRR 0.87 [95% CI: 0.78-0.97]). Among all patients with bacteremia, 30-day mortality demonstrated no significant differences pre- vs. post-intervention (adjusted hazard ratio = 0.92 [95% CI: 0.56-1.51]). In contrast, in severe bacteremia (Pitt bacteremia score >= 4), pharmacist-driven stewardship was associated with lower 30-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio = 0.52 [95% CI: 0.28-0.99]). Furthermore, Sawada et al. evaluated a noncertified pharmacist-led ASP in a 313-bed community hospital without ID specialists using PAF in a retrospective pre-post design. After ASP implementation, the median length of stay significantly decreased from 14.8 to 13.8 days (odds ratio [OR] = 0.91 [95% CI: 0.88-0.95]). In addition, process measures improved, including shorter length of therapy (median, 6 [interquartile range (IQR) 2-10] to 6 [IQR 2-9] days; OR = 0.92 [95% CI: 0.88-0.96]) and reduced empiric use of antipseudomonal/anti-MRSA agents (27.9-25.3%; OR = 0.88 [95% CI: 0.80-0.95]). Notably, the 30-day mortality (5.1% vs. 5.1%) and 30-day readmission (5.0% vs. 5.1%) exhibited no significant differences between periods. These reports indicate that pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship interventions in small- to medium-sized hospitals reduce the use of broad-spectrum antimicrobials and may improve patient outcomes.
Pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship for outpatients

According to a report from the AMR Clinical Reference Center in Japan, hospital antibiotic consumption in 2020 (difference-in-differences [DIDs]; defined daily doses [DDD] per 1,000 inhabitants per day) was 0.675 for inpatient parenteral antimicrobials, 0.371 for inpatient oral antimicrobials, 0.018 for outpatient parenteral antimicrobials, and 2.214 for outpatient oral agents. Overall antibiotic use was higher in outpatients than in inpatients, with outpatient oral antibiotics accounting for the largest proportion. Therefore, from a macro-level perspective, optimizing antibiotic use is crucial in outpatient settings. Table 1 presents the core elements of outpatient antimicrobial stewardship. The core elements for promoting appropriate antimicrobials in outpatient settings are categorized into commitment, action for policy and practice, tracking and reporting, and education and expertise. In Japan, hospital ASTs primarily focus on supporting the appropriate use of antimicrobials, mainly for parenteral agents within each facility, as described above; however, the initiatives to promote the appropriate use of antimicrobials among outpatients at their institutions are also increasingly being implemented.

General medical practice

In a single-center outpatient stewardship project at a Japanese university hospital, Ebihara et al. showed that routine AST activities directed at outpatients, including the monthly monitoring of oral antimicrobial use, the identification of unnecessary prescriptions for acute respiratory infections and acute diarrhea, feedback to high-prescription departments via "linked doctor" meetings, and multidisciplinary education, were associated with measurable improvements in prescriptions. Over 2 years, the total oral antibiotic consumption decreased (DDDs/1,000 outpatients 339.99   324.21), with marked reductions in third-generation cephalosporins (18.97   13.14 DDDs) and fluoroquinolones (39.12   33.53), and the proportion of clearly unnecessary prescriptions for targeted syndromes declined over time. In outpatient settings, stewardship extends beyond syndromic management to condition-specific optimization of antimicrobial regimens and duration. We evaluated a pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship intervention for clarithromycin-resistant Helicobacter pylori, where pharmacists reviewed culture and susceptibility results and recorded (electronically) regimen recommendations before first-line eradication therapy. The comparisons of the pre-intervention (2015-2018) and stewardship (2019-2020) periods showed that initial eradication success with vonoprazan-based regimens improved from 80.0% (116 out of 145) to 94.9% (37 out of 39), while the median total drug cost per successfully eradicated patient decreased from 6,624.7 to 6,392.3 yen, reflecting decreased treatment failures and cumulative antibiotic exposure. In a repeated cross-sectional study from a Japanese community hospital, Tsuchimoto et al. showed that an ASP formally targeting only inpatients nonetheless altered outpatient oral prescription patterns. Between 2013 and 2019, the proportion of appropriate outpatient treatments increased from 68.4% to 83.7%, and third-generation cephalosporin prescriptions per 1,000 outpatients decreased from 21.4 to 6.3, with compensatory increases in penicillins and co-trimoxazole. These findings suggest a "spillover" effect of inpatient-focused antimicrobial stewardship on outpatient prescription; however, the use of fluoroquinolone and prophylactic also increased.
Dental practice

Tagashira Y et al. implemented a pharmacist-led intervention in a dental university hospital, providing feedback with real-time review and recommendations for in-hospital prescriptions and electronic medical record-based message feedback for outpatient (external) prescriptions, along with mini-lectures for dental students. Consequently, the monthly mean proportion of prescriptions for penicillins increased from 45.6 to 84.1 per 100 oral antimicrobial prescriptions (P < 0.001), while that of third-generation cephalosporins decreased from 43.0 to 7.3 (P < 0.001) from the pre-intervention to the intervention period. Endo et al. assessed a pharmacist-led outpatient ASP in a dental/oral surgery department (pre-intervention: October 2018 to September 2020; post-intervention: October 2020 to September 2022). The intervention included distributing an antibiotic reference table (bioavailability, indications, renal-dose recommendations, costs, and guidance from the Japanese Association for Infectious Diseases/Japan Society of Chemotherapy infection guideline) and informing dentists of the baseline prescription patterns. Two pharmacists provided real-time prescription support, including recommending penicillins per guidelines, proposing Pharmacokinetics/renal function-based dosing, and suggesting alternatives for allergies (e.g., switching to clarithromycin), with additional consultation at the time of antibiotic changes/prescription. After implementation, prescription shifted from third-generation cephalosporins toward penicillins (15%   48% for penicillins; 64%   36% for third-generation cephalosporins; P < 0.05), and cefditoren pivoxil antimicrobial use density (AUD) significantly decreased from 139.3 to 82.3 (P < 0.05), while amoxicillin AUD increased from 22.2 to 62.7.
Community-wide antimicrobial stewardship

Community-wide antimicrobial stewardship is essential because population-level antibiotic consumption, which is largely driven by outpatient/community prescriptions, has been associated with high rates of antimicrobial resistance, indicating that reducing unnecessary use in the community may curb resistance selection. In addition, inappropriate antibiotic prescription increases patient complications, including antibiotic-associated adverse events and Clostridioides difficile infection, highlighting that stewardship is a core intervention for patient safety. Therefore, the region-wide optimization of antibiotic prescription is required to mitigate resistance pressure and reduce avoidable antibiotic-related complications. According to a report from the AMR Clinical Reference Center, the total antibiotic consumption in 2020 based on DDDs per 1,000 inhabitants per day was 3.279 in hospitals, whereas it was 7.433 in clinics (including clinics with < 19 beds); most of this consumption was attributable to oral antibiotics. In a randomized control trial-based meta-analysis, audit and feedback Interventions were associated with an 11% relative reduction in antibiotic prescription volume (rate ratio [RR] = 0.89; 95% CI: 0.84-0.95), 23% relative reduction in unnecessary antibiotic initiation (n = 16 studies, RR = 0.77; 95% CI: 0.68- 0.87), 13% relative reduction in prolonged duration of antibiotic course (n = 4 studies, RR = 0.87 95% CI: 0.81-0.94), and 17% relative reduction in broad-spectrum antibiotic selection (n = 17 studies, RR = 0.83 95% CI: 0.75-0.93. However, analyses on the specific details or frequency of the audit-and-feedback interventions are lacking. This cross-sectional study of nationwide primary care clinics in Japan showed that higher-volume clinics, solo practices, and clinics owned by older physicians were more likely to prescribe antibiotics, particularly broad-spectrum antibiotics, for nonbacterial acute respiratory infections. To promote appropriate prescription through an ASP targeting clinics outside one's institution, a randomized control trial was used to evaluate three behavioral interventions implemented alone or in combination, namely suggested alternatives presented in electronic order sets (including nonantibiotic treatment options), accountable justification prompting clinicians to enter free-text conditions for antibiotic prescription in the electronic health records, and peer comparison emails benchmarking the prescription rates of clinicians against those of "top performers." The study reported that accountable justification (DIDs, -7.0% [95% CI: -9.1% to -2.9%]) and peer comparison (DIDs, -5.2% [95% CI: -6.9% to -1.6%]) were more effective than the other strategy. Thus, rather than indicating that static or dynamic feedback is inherently superior, these findings suggest that feedback is a key driver of behavior change. In Japan, the proportion of physicians who were unaware of the AMR Action Plan or the Manual of Antimicrobial Stewardship was approximately 40% in 2018 and remained approximately 30-35% in 2020. Moreover, physicians who changed their antibiotic prescription patterns tend to be highly familiar with the AMR Action Plan and the stewardship manual. In contrast, when the impact of the nationwide dissemination of The Manual of Antimicrobial Stewardship, issued by Japan's Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare in June 2017, was evaluated, no significant changes were detected in antibiotic-use trends among outpatients with acute respiratory tract infections or gastroenteritis. This suggests that merely publishing clinical guidance is insufficient and that active efforts to promote awareness and uptake are required. Providing feedback based on surveillance data and improving the understanding of clinicians regarding the AMR Action Plan and antimicrobial stewardship guidance may facilitate appropriate antimicrobial use at the community level.
Hospital AST-led community intervention

Inoue et al. reported that the AST-led community intervention involves lectures aimed at optimizing antimicrobial use, the regular publication of surveillance data of drug-resistant strains at the Japan Red Cross Ishikawa Hospital, and the presentation of first-line treatments for community-acquired infections. Consequently, the delivery of oral antimicrobials across the region in 2020 was lower than that in 2013 by 28.7%, with the delivery of cephalosporins, quinolones, and macrolides decreasing by 34.8%, 46.8%, and 56.0%, respectively. In addition, we conducted interventions aimed at changing the physicians' prescription patterns of oral broad-spectrum antimicrobials (particularly third-generation cephalosporins, quinolones, and macrolides) and promoting the use of narrow-spectrum agents, such as penicillins; these interventions were operationalized through eight quarterly lectures held every 3 months between April 2022 and September 2024 and delivered by ID pharmacists to the managing physicians at community clinics. During these lectures, they provided an overview of Japan's National Action Plan for appropriate antibiotic use; gave guidance on selecting antimicrobials, primarily amoxicillin, for airway bronchiolitis and acute pharyngitis per the Manual of Antimicrobial Stewardship; explained the WHO AWaRe (Access, Watch, and Reserve) classification and its significance; and presented antimicrobial use surveillance data to enable peer comparison in the Seto-Asahi area. Using ITS analysis, the DOT for penicillins showed a statistically significant increasing trend from Period 1 (prepromoting community antimicrobial stewardship) to Period 2 (promoting community antimicrobial stewardship); the slope changed was from - 0.24 to 0.13 (P = 0.03). The DOT for the Access group increased from 2.03 (10.7%) in Period 1 to 4.05 (18.9%) in Period 2 (P < 0.01). At the national level, a comprehensive evaluation that considers the AMR Action Plan, the dissemination of the Manual of Antimicrobial Stewardship, and the nationwide implementation of financial incentives has shown a downward trend in population-adjusted antibiotic prescription/consumption.
Community pharmacy-led intervention

Nakamura et al. conducted a single-center quasi-experimental study in a community pharmacy (February 2021 to January 2023), where in February 2022, pharmacists began to suggest switching oral third-generation cephalosporins to guideline-recommended agents for conditions where these drugs were not first-line. After the intervention, antimicrobial consumption decreased markedly (median AUD 10.0   2.6; DOT 19.5   6.2; DDD/1000 prescriptions/month 9.1   2.6; all P < 0.001).

The proportion of antimicrobial prescriptions containing oral third-generation cephalosporins decreased from 84.7% to 19.8%, with compensatory increases in first-generation cephalosporins (0.9%   56.6%) and penicillins (0%   4.7%). Clinical effectiveness was maintained: antibiotic changes owing to treatment failure were 0% before and after the shift, and recurrence during follow-up decreased from 14.1% to 6.7% (P = 0.145).
Conclusions

Pharmacist-led antimicrobial stewardship has been implemented across inpatient, outpatient, and community settings. This narrative review provides an overview of the specific interventions and their outcomes. For inpatients, many reports have demonstrated consistent benefits, including improvements in clinical outcomes. In contrast, stewardship efforts targeting outpatients and community clinics remain insufficient, necessitating further intervention. These settings represent key areas where pharmacists are expected to play a greater role, particularly through rigorous evaluation that includes patient-centered outcomes.

passages.text: Grass carp reovirus VP35 hijacks DHX15 into phase-separated inclusion bodies to evade host antiviral immunity

Many viral proteins undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form biomolecular condensates known as viral inclusion bodies (VIBs), which are utilized for genome replication and virion assembly, thus serving as potential targets for antiviral drugs. However, the role of VIBs in viral immune evasion has rarely been explored. In this study, we demonstrated that VP35 protein of type II grass carp reovirus (GCRV-II) formed VIBs through LLPS in cells and in vitro. Moreover, we identified a host interaction partner of GCRV-II VP35, DEAH (Asp-Glu-Ala-His)-box helicase 15 (DHX15), which promoted expression of GCRV-II- or poly(I: C)-induced interferon (IFN) and interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) via promoting phosphorylation of TBK1 (TANK-binding kinase 1) and stabilizing TBK1 to prevent it from degradation through autophagy pathway. To evade host anti-viral immunity, GCRV-II VP35 sequesters DHX15 from nucleus to the cytoplasm VIBs and degrades DHX15 via lysosomal pathway. Our findings provide a novel immune evasion strategy of GCRV-II, of which VP35 protein recruits DHX15, a positive regulator of host anti-viral immunity, to VIBs and degrades DHX15 via lysosomal pathway, which provides novel insights for the development of anti-viral drugs against GCRV-II infection.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12964-026-02723-4.
Introduction

A prevalent feature observed during the infection processes of many viruses is the formation of a specialized compartment for genome replication and virion assembly, commonly known as viral inclusion bodies (VIBs) or viral factories (also referred to as viroplasms, replication organelles, and Negri bodies). Targeting the formation of VIBs presents a promising strategy for developing antiviral drugs. For instance, the human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) VIBs can be disrupted and solidified by the targeting drugs, thus suppressing virus replication. The VIBs of positive-strand RNA viruses are mainly formed by rearrangement of cellular membrane, including the formation of double-membrane vesicles, spherules, or invaginated vesicles. However, recent studies have indicated that some positive-strand RNA viruses, such as human norovirus, formed liquid-like membrane-less VIBs rather than membrane-associated VIBs. Likewise, for several negative-strand RNA viruses (e.g., Filoviridae), double-stranded RNA viruses (e.g., Reoviridae), and double-stranded DNA viruses (e.g., Adenoviridae), the VIBs are shown to be membrane-less biomolecular condensates formed through a process called liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).

LLPS is a phenomenon driven by multivalent protein-protein (or protein-RNA) interactions to form liquid-like condensates that stably coexist with the surrounding environment. The liquid-like condensates typically have a spherical shape with dynamic properties, e.g. fusion, fission, and fluorescence recovery after bleaching. These condensates offer a highly efficient way to spatially and temporally control a remarkable array of cellular processes, including transcription, autophagy, heterochromatin formation, and stress granule assembly. Besides, LLPS also plays an important role in virus infection. The formation of VIBs by viral proteins via LLPS has been described for RNA and recently also for DNA viruses. Initially, the formation of VIBs via LLPS, driven by the viral nucleoprotein (N) and phosphoprotein (P), was demonstrated in Mononegavirales with a negative-strand RNA genome, such as measles virus (Mev), rabies virus (RABV), mumps virus (Muv), and RSV. Ebola virus (EBOV) VIBs, a liquid-like organelles formed by N protein, responsible for the replication and genome encapsidation. The VIBs of rotavirus (RV), as sites for genome replication and sub-particle assembly, are formed through LLPS of NSP5 and NSP2. In addition to being important for virus replication, LLPS also plays a crucial role in facilitating virus escape from host monitoring. Viruses exploit LLPS to trap key host factors within the antiviral immune pathways, thereby modulating the IFN response. The nonstructural proteins (NSs) from severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) form liquid-like VIBs that trap mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) and melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) to block RNA sensing and IFN production. RABV P protein binds and sequesters TBK1 to VIBs, thereby inhibiting IFN induction. Nevertheless, the role of GCRV-II VIBs in regulating the host immune response remains poorly understood.

passages.text: DHX15 is an outstanding member of the DEAD (Asp-Glu-Ala-Asp)-box helicase family. There have been several studies claiming that mammalian DHX15 is involved in virus-induced innate immunity as an RNA virus sensor. For instance, DHX15 functions as an RNA virus sensor in dendritic cells (DCs), where it induces type I IFN in response to RNA virus, in a MAVS-dependent manner. Another study identified DHX15 as an RNA virus sensor in intestinal epithelial cells (IECs), where it regulates intestinal inflammation induced by enterovirus infection through the production of type I/III IFNs and inflammasome cytokines.

The etiological agent of the grass carp hemorrhagic disease is primarily the type II grass carp reovirus (GCRV-II). It is a non-enveloped double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus with a genome of 11 double-stranded RNA segments and replicates its genome within VIBs. In a previous study, we found that VP56 and VP35 induced the formation of GCRV-II VIBs. In the present study, we aimed to investigate the mechanism of GCRV-II VIBs biogenesis and the role of GCRV-II VIBs in immune regulation. By employing cellular and purified protein systems, we found that GCRV-II VIBs were liquid-like membrane-less condensates that formed through LLPS driven by VP35. Moreover, we identified a host protein, DHX15, that interacts with VP35 and positively regulates IFN production upon GCRV-II infection and intracellular poly(I: C) stimulation. Mechanistically, DHX15 interacted with TBK1 to promote TBK1 phosphorylation and stabilization, thus enhancing IFN production. To evade the host immune response, VP35 sequestered DHX15 into VIBs and degraded DHX15 through the lysosomal pathway. Our findings demonstrate the formation mechanism of GCRV-II VP35-mediated VIBs, providing a novel immune evasion strategy of GCRV-II.
Results
GCRV-II VP35 undergoes LLPS to form liquid-like vibs

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) previously revealed membrane-less cytoplasmic VIBs harboring a large number of virions in GCRV-II-infected cells. In this study, we analyzed the liquid-like property of VP56- and VP35-induced VIBs in grass carp ovary (GCO) cells as VP56 and VP35 of GCRV-II has previously been reported to form VIBs. Using live-cell imaging, we observed that the VIBs induced by VP35, rather than those induced by VP56, were round, mobile, and fused over minutes (Fig. 1A). Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) showed that VP35-induced VIBs exhibited a rapid and most (70%) fluorescence recovery, while VP56-induced VIBs recovered to less than 8% (Fig. 1B-D). We next analyzed the sensitivity of VIBs to aliphatic alcohol 1,6-Hex, a compound that led to dissolution of LLPS by disrupting weak hydrophobic interactions. Treatment with 2% 1,6-Hex for 3 min led to the complete dissolution of VIBs formed by VP35. However, the VIBs induced by VP56 were not affected (Fig. 1E). Additionally, treatment with 2% 1,6-Hex for 3 min exhibited no cell cytotoxicity (Fig. S1A). To further determine whether the VIBs generated by VP35 in GCRV-II-infected cells also possess the liquid-like property, GCO cells were transfected with EGFP-VP35, followed by GCRV-II infection. Live-cell imaging revealed that the VIBs generated by VP35 in GCRV-II-infected cells were mobile and fused over minutes (Fig. S1B). These results indicate that GCRV-II VP35-induced VIBs are liquid organelles formed by LLPS.

Live-cell confocal images were obtained at 24 h post-transfection. B GCO cells were transfected with pEGFP-VP56 or pEGFP-VP35 (1.0 microg each) and performed FRAP at 24 h post-transfection. White arrows indicate areas that were bleached. C-D FRAP quantification of VP35-EGFP (C) or VP56-EGFP (D) condensates in vivo before and after photobleaching within a period of 400 s. E GCO cells were transfected with pEGFP-VP56 or pEGFP-VP35 plasmids (200 ng each). The cells were imaged during treatment with 2% 1,6-Hex
GCRV-II VP35 undergoes LLPS in vitro

To test whether VP35 undergoes LLPS outside the cellular environment, we purified recombinant EGFP-VP35 fusion protein and recombinant VP35 protein using Ni-NTA agarose beads (Fig. S2A). Purified EGFP protein was used as a control, and it does not induce self-driven LLPS (Fig. S2B-C). We then investigated the LLPS property of VP35 under different environmental concentrations in vitro. The purified VP35 protein with a concentration of 150 ng/microL formed droplets in 50 mM NaCl solution at a temperature of 25C and pH values range of 5.5-9.0 (Fig. 2A-C). Increasing the NaCl concentration to 400 mM abolished the formation of droplets at protein concentrations between 150 ng/microL and 300 ng/microL. Increasing the VP35 protein concentration to 450 ng/microL or 600 ng/microL facilitated phase separation even at high salt (400 mM NaCl) condition (Fig. 2A). Within the range of VP35 protein concentration from 150 ng/microL to 600 ng/microL, no droplets were observed at 4C and pH 2.0 (Fig. 2B and C). To test whether the observed droplet formation was dependent on weak interaction, the proteins were subjected to 1,6-Hex, heat inactivation, and proteinase K, respectively. VP35 droplet formation was abrogated by 5% 1,6-Hex, heat inactivation, or proteinase K (Fig. 2D), confirming that LLPS of VP35 was due to weak protein-protein interactions. In addition, purified recombinant His-tagged VP35 was used for in vitro phase separation assay with 10% polyethylene glycol 8000 (PEG8000), a crowing agent used for in vitro LLPS investigation. By using differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy, we found that purified His-VP35 proteins formed spherical droplets at NaCl concentrations ranging from 50 mM to 500 mM in the presence of 10% PEG8000 (Fig. 2E). Altogether, these findings indicate that purified VP35 protein can undergo LLPS in vitro.

GCRV-II VP35 undergoes LLPS in vitro. A-C Droplet formation (left) and phase separation (PS) diagram (right) of EGFP-labelled VP35 (150 ng/microL) at room temperature with the indicated concentrations of NaCl at pH 5.5 (A), 50 mM NaCl at pH 5.5 at the indicated temperatures B, and at the indicated pH conditions with 50 mM NaCl at room temperature C. D 150 ng/microL EGFP-VP35 were treated with 5% Hex, heated-inactivated (5 min at 95C and immediately put on ice for 5 min), or treated with 100 microg/mL Proteinase K for 30 min at 40C, and then subjected to phase separation assay in vitro (50 mM NaCl, pH 5.5, room temperature). E Brightfield images of 250 ng/microL His-VP35 in phase separation assay buffer with 10% PEG8000 upon the indicated concentrations of NaCl
DHX15 interacts with VP35

To explore whether VP35-induced VIBs functions for immune escape, an immunoprecipitation (IP) assay was performed on pEGFP-VP35-transfected GCO cells using anti-EGFP agarose beads. The GCO cells transfected with pEGFP-N1 (the empty vector) were used as control. The eluted samples were analyzed by Western blotting and silver staining (Fig. 3A). Several proteins essential for viral replication, such as vimentin, HSP60, DHX15, and cyclophilin A, were detected in the EGFP-VP35 sample but not from the control sample (Fig. 3B). By Co-IP assays, we examined the interaction of vimentin, heat shock protein 60 (HSP60), DHX15, and cyclophilin A with VP35, respectively. The results showed that DHX15, but not the other proteins, interacted with VP35 (Fig. 3C and S3). It has been reported that mammalian DHX15 acts as an important RNA sensor in triggering the production of IFN. However, the role of grass carp DHX15 in antiviral immunity has not been reported. Therefore, DHX15 was selected in this study.

DHX15 interacts with VP35. A GCO cells were transfected with pEGFP-N1 (control) or pEGFP-VP35 (10 microg each), and the cells were collected at 24 h post-transfection. IP assay was performed using an anti-EGFP antibody. The eluted samples were detected by Western blotting and silver staining. B The samples from (A) were analyzed by LC-MS/MS, and the potential interacting proteins previously reported involved in virus replication were listed. C 293T cells were transfected with pCMV-Flag and pEGFP-VP35 (5.0 microg each), or pCMV-Flag-DHX15 and pEGFP-VP35 (5.0 microg each). The cells were collected at 24 h post-transfection, followed by Co-IP assay with anti-Flag antibody
VP35 recruits DHX15 to the VIBs

Next, we assessed the intracellular localization patterns of DHX15 and VP35. Transfection of Flag-DHX15 alone showed that DHX15 was localized in the nucleus. When co-transfected with EGFP-VP35, DHX15 could be detected in VP35-induced VIBs in the cytoplasm (Fig. 4A). To determine whether DHX15 was localized in VIBs in GCRV-II infected cells, GCO cells were transfected with Flag-DHX15, followed with or without GCRV-II infection. We found that DHX15 showed a nuclear localization in GCO cells when expressed alone, but co-localized in VIBs with VP35 in the cytoplasm of GCRV-II infected cells (Fig. 4B), indicating that VP35 recruited DHX15 to VIBs in both transfected and infected cells. To further substantiate these results, we analyzed the localization of endogenous DHX15 upon GCRV-II infection (Fig. 4C). Similarly, endogenous DHX15 was localized in the nucleus without GCRV-II infection. Whereas, endogenous DHX15 was co-localized with VP35 in cytoplasmic VIBs during GCRV-II infection. These data suggest that VP35 recruits DHX15 from nucleus to the cytoplasmic VIBs.

VP35 recruits DHX15 to the VIBs. A GCO cells were transfected with pFlag-DHX15 and pEGFP-N1 (control) (1.0 microg each) or pFlag-DHX15 together with pEGFP-VP35 (1.0 microg each). At 24 h transfection, the cells were fixed and stained with polyclonal antibody against Flag. B GCO cells were transfected with pFlag-DHX15 (1.0 microg) and then infected with or without GCRV-II. At 48 h post-infection, the cells were fixed and stained with polyclonal antibodies against Flag and VP35. C GCO cells were infected with or without GCRV-II. At 48 h post-infection, the cells were fixed and stained with polyclonal antibodies against DHX15 and VP35. The samples were detected using confocal microscope
DHX15 positively regulates IFN response upon GCRV-II infection and intracellular poly(I: C) stimulation

To investigate the response of cellular DHX15 during GCRV-II infection, GCO cells were infected with GCRV-II, and the mRNA and protein levels of DHX15 were measured at different time points after infection. The mRNA level of DHX15 was increased to about two-fold at 24 h post-infection (hpi), followed by gradually increasing to the peak level at 72 hpi (Fig. 5A). Consistently, GCRV-II infection resulted in a great increase of DHX15 proteins along with the time points (Fig. 5B). Previous studies have shown that mammalian DHX15 interacts with MAVS for promoting IFN-I production. We therefore hypothesized whether grass carp DHX15 played a role in regulating IFN response. To test this hypothesis, we evaluated its potential to affect the transcription of grass carp IFN1 and ISGs upon GCRV-II infection and intracellular poly(I: C) stimulation. As shown in Fig. 5C and D, compared to the control cells transfected with empty vector pCMV-Flag, transfection of pFlag-DHX15 in GCO cells enhanced the transcription of cellular IFN1, ISG15, and Mx2 induced by intracellular poly(I: C) or GCRV-II stimulation. These results suggest that DHX15 positively regulates the IFN pathway stimulated by poly(I: C) or GCRV-II, indicating a positive role of DHX15 in teleost antiviral immunity. To further explore the role of DHX15 in viral replication, GCO cells were transfected with Flag-DHX15, followed by GCRV-II infection. The results showed that overexpression of DHX15 inhibited GCRV-II replication by detecting the viral protein and mRNA levels (Fig. 5E and F). Similarly, fewer copies of GCRV-II were detected in the supernatant of DHX15-overexpressed cells (Fig. 5G). All these results indicate that DHX15 inhibits GCRV-II replication by enhancing IFN response.

A The cellular mRNA levels of DHX15 were measured by qRT-PCR. B The protein levels of DHX15 were determined by Western blotting. beta-actin was used as the internal control. C-D qRT-PCR analysis of IFN1 and ISGs mRNAs in GCO cells. GCO cells seeded in 12-well plates overnight were infected with GCRV-II (C) or transfected with poly(I: C) (1.0 microg/mL) (D), then cells were harvested for qRT-PCR. E-G GCO cells were transfected with pCMV-Flag (empty vector) or pFlag-DHX15 (1.0 microg each) for 24 h. At 24 h post-transfection, GCO cells were infected with GCRV-II. At 48 h post-infection, the viral VP4 mRNA (E) and NS38 protein (F) were detected by qRT-qPCR and Western blotting, and the number of virions in supernatants was measured by absolute quantification G. Null: null transaction. All the data are representative of at least two independent experiments, with each determination performed in triplicate (mean +- SD). * and ** indicate statistically significant differences (*, p < 0.05; **, p < 0.01)
DHX15 promotes IFN response by targeting TBK1

To further explore the components of the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling pathway that interact with DHX15, Co-IP assays were applied. As indicated in Fig. 6A, DHX15 was found to be associated with MAVS, MITA, TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7. Subsequently, we further investigate which component of the RLR signaling pathway was targeted by DHX15. The transcripts of grass carp IFN1 were effectively induced by the overexpression of each pivotal component of the RLR signaling pathway, including MAVS, MITA, TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7. Moreover, DHX15 could further significantly enhance the transcripts of grass carp IFN1 induced by TBK1, but not MAVS, MITA, IRF3, or IRF7 (Fig. 6B). Further assay revealed that overexpression of DHX15 positively regulated the TBK1-induced production of IFN1 in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 6C). These results indicate that DHX15 promotes IFN response by targeting TBK1.

DHX15 promotes IFN response by targeting TBK1. A 293T cells seeded in 25-cm2 dishes overnight were transfected with pFlag-DHX15 (5.0 microg) and the molecules of RLR signaling pathway, including RIG-I, MAVS, MITA, TBK1, IRF3, and IRF7 (5.0 microg each). The cells were collected at 24 h post-transfection, followed by Co-IP assay with anti-Myc antibody. B GCO cells seeded in 12-well plates overnight were co-transfected with empty vector (pCMV-Flag) or pFlag-DHX15 (1.0 microg each), and key component plasmids (MAVS, MITA, TBK1, IRF3, IRF7) (1.0 microg each) of RLRs signaling pathway. At 24 h post-transfection, cells were collected for qRT-PCR. C GCO cells seeded in 12-well plates overnight were co-transfected with TBK1 (1.0 microg each) and increasing DHX15 (0 microg, 0.5 microg, 1 microg, 2 microg). At 24 h post-transfection, cells were collected for qRT-PCR
DHX15 interacts with TBK1

We further investigated the subcellular localization of DHX15 and TBK1 in GCO cells. The results demonstrated that DHX15 alone was dispersed in the nucleus but co-localized in the cytoplasm when co-transfected with Myc-TBK1 (Fig. 7A). To pinpoint the domain of DHX15 responsible for its interaction with TBK1, full-length DHX15 was divided into five truncated forms in accordance with the functional region analysis by SMART software (Fig. 7B). Co-IP assays indicated that all the truncated forms of DHX15 interacted with TBK1 (Fig. 7C and D), suggesting that the interaction between DHX15 and TBK1 was independent of a specific functional region of DHX15.

DHX15 interacts with TBK1. A GCO cells seeded onto glass coverslips in 12-well plates overnight were transfected with pFlag-DHX15 and pMyc-TBK1 (1.0 microg each) individually or collectively. The cells were fixed and stained with polyclonal antibodies against Flag or Myc. B The schematic shows the plasmids expressing different DHX15 truncated forms. C-D The plasmid pMyc-TBK1 (5.0 microg) was co-transfected with plasmids expressing Flag-tagged DHX15 truncations (5.0 microg each) into 293T cells. At 24 h post-transfection, cell lysate was collected and subjected to Co-IP with anti-Flag (C) or anti-Myc (D) antibody
DHX15 enhances IFN response by promoting TBK1 phosphorylation and stabilization

To elucidate the underlying mechanism by which DHX15 enhances IFN response via targeting TBK1, the effect of DHX15 on the transcription of TBK1 in GCO cells was investigated. As shown in Fig. 8A, overexpression of DHX15 did not alter the TBK1 transcripts in GCO cells. To determine whether DHX15 regulates the stability of the TBK1 protein, GCO cells were transfected with pMyc-TBK1, together with or without pFlag-DHX15 for 18 h and then cultured with a protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX, 25 microg/mL). As shown in Fig. 8B, treatment with CHX led to a reduction of TBK1 protein, whereas the presence of DHX15 compensated the reduction of TBK1 protein, indicating that DHX15 specifically maintained the stability of TBK1. To explore which pathway was involved in the degradation of TBK1, MG132 (a proteasome inhibitor), NH4Cl (a lysosomal inhibitor), and 3-MA (an autophagy inhibitor) were used. The results showed that DHX15 showed no significant effect on TBK1 degradation when 3-MA was used (Fig. 8C), indicating that DHX15 maintained the stability of TBK1 to avoid its degradation via autophagy pathway. TBK1 is a key kinase in the innate immune response and promotes IFN production by triggering the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of IRF3. The phosphorylation of TBK1 is indispensable for its function. Therefore, we explored whether DHX15 modulates TBK1 activity by promoting its phosphorylation. We co-transfected Myc-TBK1 with or without Flag-DHX15 into GCO cells, and the pull-down experiment was performed with anti-panPhosphoSerine/Threonine beads. The results showed that DHX15 dramatically increased phosphorylation of TBK1 (Fig. 8D). Our data suggest that DHX15 enhances IFN expression via promoting TBK1 phosphorylation and stabilizing TBK1 to prevent it from degradation via autophagy pathway.

DHX15 enhances IFN response by activating and stabilizing TBK1. A GCO cells seeded in 12-well plates were co-transfected with pMyc-TBK1 (1.0 microg) and increasing amounts of pFlag-DHX15 (0, 1, 2 microg) for 24 h, followed by qRT-PCR to analyze the expression of TBK1 at the mRNA levels. B-C Plasmid pMyc-TBK1 (2.0 microg) was transfected into GCO cells, together with pCMV-Flag or pFlag-DHX15 (2.0 microg each). At 24 h post-transfection, the cells were treated with CHX for 5 h and 7 h (B), or the indicated inhibitors (5 microM MG132, 15 microM NH4Cl, or 60 microM 3-MA) for 8 h (C), and then harvested to detect the indicated proteins using Western blotting. beta-actin was used as the internal control. The integrated optical densities of the protein bands were measured using Image-Pro Plus 6.0. D GCO cells seeded in 25-cm2 dishes overnight were transfected with pFlag-DHX15 and pMyc-TBK1 (5.0 microg each). At 24 h post-transfection, cell lysate was collected and subjected to IP with anti-panPhosphoSerine/Threonine antibody
VP35 hijacks DHX15 to inhibit innate immune response

To further investigate whether VP35 disrupts the anti-GCRV-II ability of DHX15, we first examined its effect on DHX15 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels. As shown in Fig. 9A, there was no significant change at the mRNA level of DHX15 when pFlag-DHX15 and pMyc-VP35 were co-transfected. However, overexpression of VP35 reduced the protein level of DHX15 in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 9B), suggesting that VP35 regulates DHX15 at the protein level. We speculate that this inhibitory effect might involve the degradation of DHX15 mediated by VP35. To test this hypothesis, we investigated the effects of MG132, NH4Cl, and 3-MA on VP35-mediated DHX15 protein expression. The results showed that the VP35-mediated downregulation of DHX15 protein was significantly restored by NH4Cl, indicating that VP35 degrades DHX15 through the lysosomal-dependent pathway (Fig. 9C). Furthermore, we established the stable knockdown of DHX15 in GCO cells through using short hairpin RNA (shRNA). The knockdown efficiency of the four shRNAs was verified, and shDHX15-1103 exhibited the most effective knockdown, reducing target expression by approximately 38% relative to the shNC control (Fig. 9D). Knockdown of DHX15 attenuated IFN response triggered by intracellular poly(I: C) stimulation (Fig. S4), further confirming DHX15 as an RLR pathway regulator. To explore the functional link between VP35 and DHX15 in immune regulation, GCO cells were transfected with shDHX15-1103 or control shRNA, together with or without intracellular poly(I: C) transfection. In cells transfected with control shRNA, poly(I: C) significantly increased IFN1 transcripts, whereas overexpression of VP35 suppressed poly(I: C)-induced IFN1 transcription. However, VP35 showed little effect on IFN1 transcription when DHX15 was knocked down (Fig. 9E), suggesting that VP35 mediated the immunosuppressive function through DHX15. These results demonstrate that GCRV-II VP35 sequesters DHX15 from nucleus to the cytoplasm VIBs and degrades DHX15 via lysosomal pathway for immune evasion.

Discussion

A hallmark of infection by double-stranded RNA virus is the formation of membrane-less VIBs via LLPS to support viral genome replication. However, the specific mechanisms driving the formation of GCRV-II VIBs and their role in regulating the host immune response remain largely unexplored. In this study, we showed that GCRV-II VIBs are phase-separated biomolecular condensates formed by phase separation of the VP35 protein. VP35 interacts with host protein DHX15, which promotes TBK1 phosphorylation and stabilizes TBK1, thereby enhancing the antiviral innate immune response. Moreover, VP35 hijacked DHX15 for immune evasion through recruiting DHX15 to VIBs and degrading DHX15 via lysosomal pathway.

In the case of dsRNA viruses, viral proteins such as NS80 of GCRV-I, NSP5 and NSP2 of RV, and NS2 of bluetongue virus (BTV) undergo phase separation to form liquid-like membrane-less condensates, suggesting that this phenomenon is widespread among Reoviridae. In our study, the GCRV-II VIBs also exhibit liquid-like properties, including spherical shapes, occurrence of fusion, and dynamic components exchange, similar to GCRV-I, RV, and BTV. In general, viral proteins require additional client proteins or nucleic acids to undergo phase separation. For example, the phase separation of RV NSP5 depends on the presence of NSP2 or poly-arginine. In contrast, for GCRV-II VIB formation, VP35 is sufficient as the major scaffold protein. However, another GCRV-II VIB-forming protein, VP56, only formed aggregate-like structures rather than liquid condensates. The possible explanation is that the punctate structures formed by VP56 expression alone are a result of self-aggregation, indicating that VP56 is not directly involved in phase separation to form GCRV-II VIBs. Interestingly, we found that the purified VP35 could undergo phase separation within the pH values range from 5.5 to 9 in vitro. Given that viral infection can alter the intracellular pH, this result implies that GCRV-II can form VIBs and maintain efficient replication under varying intracellular pH conditions.

In this study, VP35 was used as a bait to capture interacting immune-associated host proteins. We identified a novel member of the IFN signaling pathway, DHX15. DHX15 was initially characterized for its major role in RNA metabolism. Recent research has demonstrated that DHX15 regulates the chikungunya virus (CHIKV) replication by controlling glycolysis in mosquito cells. Increasing evidence has established DHX15 as a viral RNA sensor or mediator for several RNA viruses, triggering an antiviral response by inducing IFN production. Consistent with these findings, we found that DHX15 enhanced IFN response triggered by intracellular poly(I: C) and GCRV-II stimulation. Further investigation revealed that DHX15 positively regulates antiviral response by maintaining TBK1 stability and promoting its phosphorylation. This mechanism differs from mammalian DHX15, which induces IFN-I production by forming a complex with MAVS. These findings reveal differences in the regulation of antiviral immune responses by DHX15 between teleosts and mammals. However, for an in-depth exploration of the DHX15-mediated antiviral immune regulatory pathway from an evolutionary perspective, systematic studies on DHX15 in amphibians and reptiles are currently lacking. Our results highlight DHX15 as a key mediator of the IFN signaling pathway in low vertebrates. However, whether DHX15 functions as an RNA sensor needs to be further investigated. To our knowledge, this is the first report of DHX15's role in innate antiviral immunity of teleost fish, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic target to reduce GCRV-II replication.

To successfully infect host cells and establish long-term latency, GCRV-II, the most prevalent and serious pathogen of grass carp hemorrhagic disease, has evolved various strategies to directly affect host immune proteins within the RLR signaling pathway. These strategies include the degradation of RIG-I or phosphorylated IRF7 by VP56, the degradation of RIG-I by VP4, the degradation of MAVS by VP3 or VP35, the inhibition of phosphorylated MITA by VP41, and the inhibition of phosphorylated IRF3/7 by NS79. Unlike previous studies, we found that VP35 sequesters DHX15 into VIBs, and degrades DHX15 via lysosomal pathway, thereby inhibiting the type I IFN response. Moreover, during intracellular poly(I: C) stimulation, VP35-mediated immune evasion is strictly dependent on DHX15. The recruitment of immune factors to VIBs as a mechanism of immune evasion has been reported in other viruses, including EBOV, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, and SARS-COV-2. Therefore, we uncovered an unrecognized strategy employed by GCRV-II for immune evasion via VP35-mediated VIBs.

Although our data indicate that VP35 can achieve immune evasion by hijacking DHX15 into VIBs and degrading DHX15, we have not yet verified whether both biological processes occured in the VIBs. Furthermore, there may be a potential mechanism where VP35 recruits lysosomes to the vicinity of VIBs, thereby completing the degradation of DHX15 in this region. Additional investigations will be required for a better understanding of the spatial-specific molecular mechanism by which VP35 regulates DHX15.
Conclusion

Our study proposes a compelling model in which GCRV-II VP35 forms liquid-like VIBs and hijacks DHX15, thereby impairing host innate immunity to facilitate viral replication and achieve immune evasion (Fig. 10). In conclusion, our findings provide valuable insight into the mechanism of GCRV-II VIB formation and the antiviral regulatory role of DHX15 in teleost fish.

Materials and methods
Cell cultures and viruses

Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells were grown in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM, Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco) at 37C with 5% CO2. Grass carp ovary (GCO) cells were grown in Medium 199 (M199, Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin at 28C. The GCRV-II strain GCRV-AH528 was propagated in GCO cells and stored in our laboratory.
Antibodies and reagents

Rabbit polyclonal antibodies against GCRV-II VP35 were prepared by AtaGenix Laboratories Co., Ltd (Wuhan, China). Antibodies against Flag (20543-1-AP), Myc (16286-1-AP), EGFP (50430-2-AP), beta-actin (20536-1-AP), and DHX15 (12265-1-AP) were purchased from Proteintech (Wuhan, China). The secondary anti-rabbit IgG (SA00001-2) and anti-mouse IgG (SA00001-1) antibodies were purchased from Proteintech. Alexa Fluor 488 AffiniPure Goat Anti-Mouse IgG (H + L) antibody (115-545-003) and Cy3-AffiniPure Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L) antibody (A0516) were purchased from Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). 1, 6-hexanediol (1,6-Hex, 240117) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Poly(I: C) (HY-107202), Cycloheximide (CHX, HY-12320), MG132 (HY-13259), 3-MA (HY-19312), NH4Cl (HY-Y1269), and PEG8000 (HY-Y0873J) were purchased from MedChem Express (MCE).
Virus infection

GCO cells at 80-90% confluency of cell monolayer were incubated with GCRV-II (GCRV-AH528 strain) for 5 h at 28C. The medium was then replaced with fresh medium containing 5% FBS and incubated for the indicated times at 28C.
Plasmid construction and transfection

The plasmids pFlag-VP35, pEGFP-VP35, and pEGFP-VP56 were constructed as previously described. The plasmid pFlag-DHX15 was constructed by inserting its corresponding open reading frame (ORF) (XM_051900649.1) into the p3xFlag-CMV-14 expression vector. The plasmids for pMyc-VP35, pMyc-RIG-I (XM_051881036.1), pMyc-MAVS (XM_051916384.1), pMyc-MITA (XM_051860766.1), pMyc-TBK1 (XM_051892287.1), pMyc-IRF3 (XM_051914094.1), and pMyc-IRF7 (XM_051884531.1) were constructed by inserting their corresponding ORFs into the pCMV-Myc expression vector. The plasmids pET-28a-VP35 and pET-28a-EGFP-C-VP35 were constructed by inserting their corresponding ORFs into the pET-28a and pET-28a-EGFP-C expression vectors. All constructs were confirmed by DNA sequencing. Primer sequences were listed in S1 Table. Polyethylenimine (PEI, Polysciences, 24765-1) was used for transient transfection of plasmids into HEK293T cells following standard protocols. Plasmids and poly(I: C) were transfected into GCO cells using Lipofectamine  2000 transfection reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11668019) according to the manufacturer's protocol.
Purification of VP35 recombinant proteins

The coding sequence of VP35 was inserted into the pET-28a plasmid and pET-28a-EGFP-C plasmid, respectively. Proteins were expressed in BL21 (DE3) system under the condition of 1 mM Isopropyl beta-D-Thiogalactoside (IPTG) induction at 16  C for 12 h. The proteins were collected and lysed with a high-pressure cracker in lysis buffer (25 mM Tris, 300 mM NaCl, pH 8). After centrifugation, the supernatant was incubated with Ni-NTA agarose beads (HQ060312025M, HUIYAN Bio), and the proteins were eluted with elution buffer (25 mM Tris, 300 mM NaCl, 300 mM imidazole, pH 8). After that, proteins were dialyzed in Tris buffer (25 mM, pH 7.5) and stored at -80C for later experiments.
Fusion assay

GCO cells were seeded on confocal dishes and transfected with indicated plasmids. After 24 h, cells were imaged and captured by high-content analysis (HCA) imaging cell-based assay system (Perkin Elmer). Images were acquired using a 60x/1.7 oil objective with Z series and time series. Time lapses were performed at 30 s intervals for 20 cycles.
Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP)

The cellular FRAP experiments were performed on Nikon laser confocal microscope (Nikon, N-STORM, Japan). GCO cells were transfected with indicated plasmids by using Lipofectamine 2000 according to the manufacturer's instructions. After 24 h, VP35 or VP56 condensates were bleached for 6 s at an intensity of 98% at 488 nm laser. Fluorescence recovery was recorded within a period of time. Images were acquired using a 100x oil objective with time series. Time lapses were performed at 30 s intervals for 20 cycles.
In vitro phase separation assay

For His-VP35 in vitro phase separation assay, 250 ng/microL recombinant His-VP35 was added to PEG8000 buffer (20 mM Tris, 10% PEG8000, pH 7.5) with varying salt concentrations. For VP35-EGFP in vitro phase separation assays, 150 ng/microL purified proteins were diluted in phase separation buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl and 1 mM dithiothreitol, and reactions were performed with the indicated salt concentrations, pH values, and temperature. After 30 min of incubation at room temperature, 10 microL reaction solution was loaded onto a glass slide, covered with a coverslip and imaged using Nikon laser confocal microscope.
Immunoprecipitation (IP) and Western blotting

The antibody for a targeted protein was conjugated to protein A/G magnetic beads (MCE, HY-K0202) at room temperature for 1 h. Plasmids-transfected cells were lysed and the cell lysate supernatant was incubated with the beads at room temperature for 1 h. The final solution was separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes (Biosharp). Membranes were blocked for 2 h at room temperature in 5% skim milk dissolved in tris-buffered saline with 0.1% tween 20 (TBST) and incubated with the indicated primary antibodies for 4 h at room temperature. The membranes were washed three times with TBST and incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit antibody or anti-mouse antibody for 1 h at room temperature. The signal intensity was then determined using Amersham Imager 600 System.
Immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy

For indirect immunofluorescence (IIF), GCO cells were seeded on 12-mm glass coverslips. On the following day, cells were transfected with indicated plasmids. The coverslips were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Beyotime, P0099-500 ml) for 20 min and permeated with 0.5% Triton X-100 (Biofroxx, 1139ML500) for 15 min. After being blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 2 h, primary antibodies diluted in 5% BSA were added at 37C for 2 h, and then secondary antibodies diluted in 5% BSA were added at 37C for 1 h. After each incubation step, cells were washed gently. DAPI staining was applied to detect the nucleus. All samples were observed using Nikon laser confocal microscope. Image acquisition and reconstruction were performed with Nikon NIS-Elements software.
Quantitative RT-PCR

Total RNA was isolated from the cells using TRIzol reagent (Vazyme Biotech, R411-01). Subsequently, the isolated RNA underwent reverse transcription into first-strand cDNA using the HiScript III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (+ gDNA wiper) (Vazyme Biotech, R312-01). Quantitative RT-PCR was performed using Hieff UNICON  Universal Blue qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd, D7601S). The expression levels were calculated using the 2-DeltaDeltaCT method, with beta-actin serving as the reference gene. Primer sequences were listed in S1 Table.
Small hairpin RNA (ShRNA) experiments

GCO cells were seeded in 12-well plates overnight and transfected with 1 microg shRNA of DHX15 or the negative control (NC) using polyethylenimine regent. ShRNAs of DHX15 and NC were obtained from genepharma (Suzhou, China). The target sequences of the shRNAs for grass carp DHX15 are listed in Table S2.
Quantification and statistical analysis

The p value was analyzed by Student t-tests using GraphPad Prism 7.0 software (GraphPad). A p value <= 0.05 was considered statistically significant and a p value > 0.05 was considered statistically non-significant (ns).
